entries.title: Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory now store conversations, extract facts, and bring long-term memory into a single AgenticRetrieveStream call. This post shows how to build a memory-aware, multi-user assistant where each user sees only the documents they may read and each user's memory stays private.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Build memory-aware AI agents with Agentic Retrieve on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

Users of a knowledge-grounded application expect it to remember them, not only to search well. They ask follow-up questions that make sense only in the context of the previous turn. They expect an answer about a policy or a procedure to reflect what they told the application about themselves last month. And they still expect every answer to be grounded in the documents they are allowed to read, with citations. Whether the application is a customer support assistant, a document chat inside a SaaS product, or an internal assistant over company policies, the expectation is the same.

Meeting that expectation is hard, because the context that would sharpen a search lives outside the knowledge base. A user’s location, role, or product tier was often mentioned in an unrelated conversation weeks ago. To use it, the application has to store every conversation, extract durable facts from it, decide which facts matter for the current question, and inject them into the request. When many users share the application, every one of those steps also has to be isolated per user, and so does every document.

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, now take over these steps: storing each conversation, extracting facts from it, and bringing the relevant facts into the search. You turn this on by adding a 

memoryConfiguration
to the 
AgenticRetrieveStream
request, which makes AgentCore memory a retrieval source alongside your knowledge base. Within the same call, the service restores the conversation, and the planner decides on its own when a fact about the user would help. It retrieves that fact from long-term memory and uses it to compose the sub-queries it sends to the knowledge base. After generating the answer, the service saves the turn back to memory. The same request carries a 
userContext
, so the knowledge base returns only the documents that the user’s access control lists (ACLs) allow. The integration is opt-in and backward compatible. Your application keeps only what is genuinely yours: authenticating the user and passing who they are.

This post shows how to build such an assistant for many users who share one knowledge base and one memory resource. Each user sees only the documents they may read, and each user’s memory stays private. The running example is an internal employee assistant for AnyCompany, a fictional company. Employees sign in with Amazon Cognito and ask questions over HR policies, IT guides, engineering runbooks, and sales plans. We show how to read the user’s identity from the Cognito ID token, how to pass it to 

AgenticRetrieveStream
for document ACLs and for memory, how to design memory namespaces for many users, and how to read the trace to see when the planner used memory. Finally, we make AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforce per-user memory isolation even when application code gets it wrong. If you deployed the application from Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, this post replaces its “persist conversation history yourself” step.

Solution overview

AnyCompany keeps its documents in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). One managed knowledge base syncs them through an ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data source. A global ACL file in the same bucket says which employees may read each folder: everyone reads HR and IT, only engineers read the engineering runbooks, and only salespeople read the commission plan. One AgentCore memory resource is shared by every employee. Amazon Cognito authenticates employees, and its ID token supplies two claims: the 

sub
(user ID) identifies the user’s memory, and the verified 
email
identifies the user to the knowledge base’s ACL filter. Three test users sign in: two engineers, Maya and Liam, and one salesperson, Sofia. The trace excerpts in this post are taken from a run of the sample application in the GitHub repository.
  • The employee signs in with Cognito and receives an ID token, a JSON Web Token (JWT) signed by the user pool.
  • The application’s API validates the token — an Amazon API Gateway JWT authorizer in production, a small FastAPI service in the sample. Unauthenticated requests do not reach the handler.
  • The handler reads two claims from the verified token: 
    sub
    becomes the memory 
    actorId
    and namespace, and 
    email
    becomes the 
    userContext.userId
    . The client body carries only 
    { question, sessionId? }
    . The handler then assumes the application’s IAM role for this user, with the session tag 
    userId=
    .
  • The handler calls 
    AgenticRetrieveStream
    with the knowledge base as the retriever, 
    userContext
    , and a 
    memoryConfiguration
    bound to this user.
  • Managed Knowledge Base restores the conversation history from short-term memory (STM) in AgentCore memory for the actor and session identified by 
    sessionBinding
    .
  • Managed Knowledge Base retrieves from the knowledge base with ACL filtering based on 
    userContext
    . It can also retrieve the user’s configured long-term memory through speculative retrieval or memory searches selected by the planner.
  • Managed Knowledge Base streams a cited answer and trace events back to the handler. The handler records the traces with a correlation ID and forwards the answer and trace information to the UI.
  • With 
    persistenceMode: DEFAULT
    , the service saves the question and generated answer to the session. AgentCore memory then extracts long-term records asynchronously according to the configured strategies.

Figure 2: One 

AgenticRetrieveStream
turn with 
userContext
and 
memoryConfiguration
. Everything between the first and last arrow is the service’s work.

Managed Knowledge Base owns ingestion, ACL filtering, indexing, ranking, planning, retrieval, and generation. With 

memoryConfiguration
, it also owns session restore, memory search, and persistence. AgentCore memory owns storage, retention, encryption, and extraction. Your application owns authentication, the UI, and reading the user’s identity from the token. There is no conversation table: when the UI lists or reopens a conversation, it reads the same memory resource.

How identity maps to the request

Every value is derived by the application from the verified ID token. None comes from the request body.

(verified, immutable in the pool)		 Which documents can be retrievedKnowledge base ACL filtering

{actorId}
in long-term namespaces		 AgentCore memory keying, plus an IAM condition

Two different claims do two different jobs. The knowledge base identifies users by email, because that is what the connected data source records in its ACLs. Memory needs an 

actorId
that never changes and is never reused. The Cognito 
sub
is both. An email address can be changed, or reassigned to a new employee after someone leaves, and that person would then inherit the old memory. You can use another stable user ID from your own user store as the 
actorId
. What matters is that it never moves to a different person.

Prerequisites

  • This walkthrough uses a managed knowledge base and an AgentCore memory resource in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2). As described in the agentic retrieval documentation, the memory resource used with this integration must be in the same AWS account as the knowledge base and in the 
    ACTIVE
    state.
  • Python 3.10 or later and Boto3 1.43.72 or later.
  • Permission to create an S3 bucket, a Cognito user pool, IAM roles, a knowledge base, and a memory resource. The sample’s 
    infra/setup.py
    creates all of these resources idempotently.

Solution walkthrough

The following steps create the knowledge base and its data source, set up the memory resource and Amazon Cognito, build the request, and read the trace to confirm the result.

Step 1: Create the knowledge base with an ACL-enabled data source

A managed knowledge base needs no vector store:

Configure the service role for your setup by following Create a service role for managed Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and pass its ARN in 

roleArn
. For model access requirements, also review the prerequisites for managed and custom models.

Documents live in the bucket under 

docs//
. Amazon S3 has no permission system of its own to crawl, so you supply the ACLs in a global ACL file in the same bucket. Each entry maps an S3 prefix to the emails that may read it:

The sample’s file also gives everyone 

docs/it/
. Then create the data source. For a managed knowledge base, every connector has the type 
MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR
, and 
connectorParameters.type
picks the source:

aclEnabled
cannot be changed after the data source is created. 
CreateDataSource
is asynchronous, so wait for the status 
AVAILABLE
. Then call 
StartIngestionJob
and wait for 
COMPLETE
. The sync reads the documents and the ACL file and indexes each document with its ACL. In the sample, all 11 documents were scanned and indexed with 0 failures. A document that no ACL entry covers is not ingested, and a user whose email matches no entry receives no results from this data source.

The same model applies to connectors that crawl permissions from the source system, such as Microsoft SharePoint, Google Drive, and Atlassian Confluence. There, the permissions come from the source, groups are resolved from the source, and the knowledge base also checks each result against the source in real time. Your application code does not change: it still passes the user’s email in 

userContext
. For the full list, see Access Control Lists awareness enablement.

Step 2: Create the memory resource and design namespaces

One memory resource serves every user. Per-user separation comes from 

{actorId}
in the namespace templates, which AgentCore memory resolves from each event at extraction time. Two choices matter.

Strategies. The two strategies extract different things. The summary strategy summarizes each conversation, so it captures facts that a user mentions in passing, such as “I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.” Those facts are what personalize a later answer about, say, PTO. The user-preference strategy extracts stated preferences into structured records (“Prefers short bullet-point answers without tables”, “Always deploys to eu-central-1 first”) and does not treat incidental mentions as preferences. Summaries give you “what we discussed.” Preferences give you “how this person wants to be answered.” Use both.

Layout. 

retrievalConfigs
accepts one entry, so a single 
namespacePath
must reach everything the planner should see for a user. Put 
{actorId}
directly under the root: 
namespacePath: "/anycompany/"
then covers the profile and every conversation summary. A layout such as 
/anycompany/profile/{actorId}
and 
/anycompany/summaries/{actorId}
would let one entry reach only one of them.

Wait for the memory to reach 

ACTIVE
. Creating the memory does not need a user or 
actorId
, so the order of Step 2 and Step 3 does not matter. Nothing is provisioned per user: a new Cognito user becomes a new actor the first time they ask a question.

Step 3: Set up Cognito and grant the application permissions

Create a user pool and an app client without a client secret. The email decides which documents a user may read, so make it required, verified, and not changeable by the user:

Mutable
cannot be changed after the pool is created. With a mutable email, a signed-in user could change their email to a colleague’s address. If your users federate from Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, map the IdP’s email to this attribute so that it matches the email in your data source’s ACLs.

The sample enables 

USER_PASSWORD_AUTH
so the local UI and tests can sign in directly. Production applications typically use Cognito managed login or AWS Amplify.

Set up an IAM role for the application. The backend assumes it once per user, with the session tag 

userId=
, and every memory statement is conditioned on that tag. This is the complete policy the sample runs with:

ListEvents
is required with 
sessionBinding
, 
RetrieveMemoryRecords
with 
retrievalConfigs
, and 
CreateEvent
when 
persistenceMode
is 
DEFAULT
. 
ListSessions
and 
ListMemoryRecords
are for the application’s own reads (conversation list and the “what memory knows about you” view), not for 
AgenticRetrieveStream
. The role’s trust policy allows 
sts:AssumeRole
, 
sts:TagSession
, and 
sts:SetSourceIdentity
from the backend’s own identity (an AWS Lambda execution role or an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task role in production). If the memory uses a customer managed key, add 
kms:Decrypt
on that key.

Step 4: Read the user from the token, then build the request

Verify the ID token and read the two claims. Only the ID token carries 

email
. The access token does not:

jwt.decode
checks the signature, the issuer (your user pool), the expiry, and the audience (your app client). For details of the claims, see Understanding the identity (ID) token. With API Gateway, a JWT authorizer does the same checks and passes the claims to your handler.

Next, get the user’s AWS credentials. The backend assumes the application role for this user and caches the session until shortly before it expires:

Every call for this user, including the memory calls that agentic retrieval makes on the caller’s behalf, now runs as 

assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user-
and carries the tag that the policy in Step 3 checks.

Decide the 

sessionId
. For a new conversation, the application generates one, such as 
"conv-" + uuid4().hex
, and returns it to the client. To continue a conversation, the client sends it back. To show a user their conversations, call 
ListSessions
with the user’s 
actorId
:

You do not need your own table that maps users to sessions. Accepting a 

sessionId
from the client is safe because short-term memory is keyed by 
(memoryId, actorId, sessionId)
, and the 
actorId
comes from the token. If Liam sends Maya’s 
sessionId
, it names a session inside Liam’s own space, which is empty. Agentic retrieval itself does not verify that the 
actorId
, 
sessionId
, or namespace you supply belong to the user who is asking, so they must never come from the client. Keep your own session table only if you need data that memory does not hold, such as conversation titles.

Then build the request:

Without 

userContext
, an ACL-enabled data source returns no results at all. Compare the request with the stateless handler it replaces:

The query before the call and the write after it are gone, and 

messages
has one element. Three rules come with 
sessionBinding
, and each is enforced with a specific 
ValidationException
. First, 
messages
carries only the current question, so you choose one history source per request. Second, 
persistenceMode: DEFAULT
(the default) writes the question and the generated answer as one event, so it requires 
generateResponse: true
. Third, 
memoryId
alone is invalid. 
persistenceMode: NONE
restores history and writes nothing, for audit or replay views.

Step 5: Update the client contract and render history

The client sends 

{ question, sessionId? }
. On a new conversation, the application generates a 
sessionId
and returns it as the first streamed frame. The client echoes it on later turns and omits it to start over.

Because the memory resource is yours, the application reads it directly to render a conversation:

Each persisted turn is exactly one event with two payloads: the user’s question and the final answer. The history therefore renders as a clean transcript and remains usable by other AgentCore memory clients.

Step 6: Verify from the trace

The trace tells you, per turn, what the knowledge base and memory did:

Trace eventWhen it appearsWhat to look at
SessionHistoryLoad

sessionBinding
is set		 
_memory_event_count
and 
_memory_message_count
, both 0 on a new session		 
SpeculativeRetrieval

retrievalMetadata
also lists 
BedrockAgentCoreMemory
. Memory items carry 
_memory_*
metadata and no text. Knowledge base items carry 
_source_uri
 
Planning
 Each iteration
actions[].memoryRetrieve
means the planner chose to search memory, with a query it composed		 
Retrieval
with 
retrievalType: BedrockAgentCoreMemory

_memory_record_count
. A count of 0 is a normal result
A memory event with 
status: FAILED

. Memory is best-effort: the request continues and the answer is generated from the knowledge base

The following runs show the behavior. Excerpts are verbatim, trimmed for length.

Document ACLs: Maya and Sofia, same question. “What is the weekly on-call stipend?” The on-call guide is in 

docs/engineering/
. Maya’s retrieval included 
docs/engineering/oncall.md
, and the answer was “500 USD or 450 EUR per week.” Sofia’s speculative retrieval and the planner’s follow-up sub-query returned only HR and sales chunks:

Her answer said that no on-call stipend is documented in the sources she can access. The application made no access decision. It passed 

userContext.userId: "sofia@example.com"
, and the knowledge base did the filtering. The reverse holds for the commission plan: Sofia gets the 12% accelerator, and Maya’s retrieval does not contain 
docs/sales/
.

Turn 1: Maya, new conversation. “How do I set up the VPN on my laptop? I’m on a Mac in the Frankfurt office.”

The answer gives the Frankfurt gateway (

vpn-fra.anycompany.example
) and the macOS steps. Afterwards, 
ListEvents
on the session shows one event with two payloads.

Turn 2: Maya, same conversation. “It keeps disconnecting every few minutes. What should I try?” The request carried only that sentence:

The planner sent 

retrieve("VPN disconnects every few minutes troubleshooting")
and 
retrieve("Cisco Secure Client macOS frequent disconnect fix")
. The answer resolved “it” and pointed at iCloud Private Relay, the macOS-specific cause in the guide. On a continued session, 
SpeculativeRetrieval
queries only the knowledge base. The long-term memory lookup in that step happens on new sessions.

Turn 3: Maya, a new conversation, later. “How many days of PTO do I get per year, and do unused days carry over?” Her office decides the answer, and she never mentioned it in this conversation. Speculative retrieval searched long-term memory with the raw question and found one record:

Knowledge base and memory items share one 

retrievalResponse
. Tell them apart by 
sourceRetriever.identifier
or by the 
_memory_*
keys. The record was the summary of her VPN conversation. That was enough: the planner went straight to the answer, which said “Since your memory indicates you’re based in the Frankfurt office … you get 30 days of PTO per year, granted in full on January 1, and any unused days must be used by March 31 of the following year.” A fact from an IT conversation personalized an HR answer.

Turn 4: Liam, new conversation, identical question. Same handler, same memory resource, a different token. Speculative retrieval found nothing about him, so the planner decided to search memory with its own query:

Liam received the table of all three offices and a request to say which one he is in. The application chooses where the planner may look. The planner decides whether to look and what to ask: a 

memoryRetrieve
action appears only when the planner decides that another memory search would help. Reading Maya’s 
sessionId
through the history endpoint with Liam’s token returned an empty list.

Figure 3: The same question from two users. Maya’s trace shows a memory hit and a Frankfurt-specific answer. Liam’s trace shows zero memory records and the generic table.

Long-term extraction is asynchronous and runs after the turn is persisted. In our run, the first record appeared 81 seconds after turn 2, but the timing is not a commitment. Design for eventual availability. A fact stated in this conversation is not guaranteed to be retrievable in the next one immediately. The sample polls 

ListMemoryRecords
before running turn 3.

Security and multi-user isolation

In this walkthrough, the application authenticates. The knowledge base filters. ACL-aware retrieval is filtering, not authorization. Take the email only from a verified ID token with 

email_verified: true
, make it immutable in the pool, and handle email reuse: if an address is reassigned to a different person, that person gets the old owner’s document access. The knowledge base fails closed: a document with no ACL, or an ACL error, means fewer results, not extra ones. If results are missing, check that the email matches the ACL entry.

Identity comes from the token (Step 4) for memory too: 

actorId
and namespace come from the verified 
sub
, never from the client.

IAM condition keys, as defense in depth. AgentCore memory exposes 

bedrock-agentcore:actorId
on 
ListEvents
, 
CreateEvent
, and 
ListSessions
, and 
bedrock-agentcore:namespacePath
on 
RetrieveMemoryRecords
and 
ListMemoryRecords
. The memory calls that agentic retrieval makes during a request are authorized against the calling identity. That is why the caller’s policy must grant those actions, and why the conditions in Step 3 apply to them. With the session assumed for Maya, a request bound to Maya’s 
actorId
proceeds normally. A request that binds Liam’s 
actorId
is the bug that this policy guards against, and it is denied at every memory operation:

Nothing was written to Liam’s memory: his session count stayed at 0. The answer was still generated from the knowledge base. Because each user has their own role session, AWS also sees which user each call is for: the caller is 

assumed-role/anycompany-assistant-app-role/user-
with 
SourceIdentity=
, which the session holder cannot change.

Two further points. The memory is a customer-owned resource that other systems in your account may also write to. Treat its contents as input, and attach an Amazon Bedrock guardrail to the request through 

policyConfiguration
. And plan the data lifecycle. Raw events expire per 
eventExpiryDuration
, but extracted records do not. A user-deletion workflow therefore covers 
DeleteEvent
for the actor’s sessions and 
DeleteMemoryRecord
under the actor’s namespace.

Observability and failure behavior

Log the full trace with a correlation ID per turn. The planner’s sub-queries are as worth auditing as its final results. 

AWS/Bedrock/KnowledgeBases
reports 
Invocations
, 
ClientErrors
, and 
TotalIterationCount
for 
Operation=AgenticRetrieveStream
. 
AWS/Bedrock-AgentCore
reports 
Invocations
, 
Latency
, 
Errors
, and 
UserErrors
per memory operation, and 
InputTokenUsage
/
OutputTokenUsage
per strategy for extraction. With Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search enabled, AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, shows a turn’s spans end to end.

Memory operations are best-effort by design. If a memory call fails or is denied, the request does not fail. The trace carries a 

FAILED
memory event with the failure message, and the turn continues without that memory. The answer is generated from the knowledge base. Decide whether your UI surfaces that degraded state.

Considerations

  • Use a stable 
    sessionId
    for the life of a conversation. The API accepts a fresh ID per request, but a fresh ID silently breaks continuity and produces one summary record per turn.
  • Use 
    namespacePath
    to reach all of a user’s long-term records. 
    retrievalConfigs
    accepts one entry with up to five 
    metadataFilters
    . 
    namespace
    matches by prefix and 
    namespacePath
    matches by hierarchy, so 
    namespacePath
    fits per-user IDs under the root. Supply namespaces fully resolved, because a template such as 
    /anycompany/{actorId}
    is rejected.
  • Expect only 
    USER
    and 
    ASSISTANT
    conversational events to be restored. Events with the 
    TOOL
    or 
    OTHER
    role that other systems write are skipped.
  • Keep sending 
    messages
    instead of 
    sessionBinding
    when your application needs to control exactly which history each request carries. For example, your existing history store may be the system of record for conversations, or you may edit or redact history before sending it. With 
    sessionBinding
    , the service restores and persists the conversation for you. You can’t combine the two in one request.
  • A request can carry up to five knowledge bases. With more than one retriever, the planner routes each sub-query based on the knowledge base 
    description
    , so write it carefully.
  • Plan for latency and cost. The session restore adds on the order of 200 milliseconds. In our runs, a full turn with one knowledge base, ACLs, and memory took 4–10 seconds with the managed model. Planning iterations drive that time, not memory. These are observed figures, not service commitments. Agentic retrieval is priced per call plus underlying retrievals, and the memory operations made during the call are billed as AgentCore memory usage. For details, see Amazon Bedrock pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing.

Clean up

Run 

python infra/teardown.py
in the sample to delete the knowledge base, the S3 bucket and its objects, the memory resource (including conversation history and long-term records), the Cognito user pool, and the IAM roles.

Conclusion

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base already gave you the retrieval stack as a service. That stack covers ingestion, document ACLs, indexing, ranking, and the planning loop in 

AgenticRetrieveStream
that turns a hard question into a cited answer. With 
memoryConfiguration
, the same call now carries the conversation and the user’s history. For a multi-user application, that removed the conversation store, the history replay, and the extraction pipeline. What remained was a short list of responsibilities. Authenticate the user and read two claims from the ID token: pass the verified email as 
userContext
so that the knowledge base filters documents, and use the 
sub
as the 
actorId
for one memory resource with 
{actorId}
-rooted namespaces. Use IAM condition keys on a per-user role session as a second line of defense that holds through the agentic path.

To get started, deploy the sample from the GitHub repository. Then read the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference, Access Control Lists awareness enablement, and Use AgentCore memory with agentic retrieval. For the retrieval loop itself, see Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base. For memory concepts, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory: Building context-aware agents.

entries.title: How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Duco, a data automation platform for tier-one banks, rebuilt its agentic AI stack on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With strict per-tenant isolation, a multi-model strategy, and an MCP skills architecture that cut context overhead by 90%, Duco cut reconciliation deployment time 10x and onboarding costs 70%.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How Duco transforms financial data automation with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Financial institutions face a critical challenge: processing massive volumes of data with speed, accuracy, and compliance while operating under some of the world’s strictest regulatory frameworks. Duco is the agentic Operations platform for financial services, serving tier-one banks and other financial institutions. It processes 20 billion transactions monthly for 200+ clients, including 7 of the top 20 banks and 10 of the top 20 asset managers. To keep pace as data processing demands grew, Duco evolved from traditional machine learning models to the agentic AI capabilities of Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. In this post, we share how Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on these services, cutting deployment time and onboarding costs while keeping each bank’s data isolated.

The challenge: Scaling intelligence in a regulated environment

Duco’s platform empowers teams to automate mission-critical data processes using AI and no-code models, handling everything from data extraction to downstream publication. It already used traditional machine learning models for predictive labeling and pattern recognition, helping banks consolidate and automate over 20,000 processes.

However, these classical machine learning approaches had inherent limitations. They required extensive historical data for training, struggled with novel scenarios, and demanded significant customization for each new use case. Most critically, they couldn’t adapt quickly to the diverse, constantly evolving data formats and business rules that characterize modern financial operations.

“The classical prediction models worked to an extent, but they weren’t agile or flexible enough. Traditional machine learning models can only amplify what they’ve already learned — they can’t help with the next step or find new problems.”

— Rob Gates, Chief Architect and Innovation Officer, Duco

The solution: Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore

Duco made a strategic decision to adopt Amazon Bedrock for managed access to foundation models, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to run agents at scale. This was more than a technology upgrade. It was a fundamental shift in how its system could understand, reason about, and act on financial data.

About Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore

Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that offers a choice of high-performing foundation models from leading AI companies through a single API, along with a broad set of capabilities to build generative AI applications with security, privacy, and responsible AI. Learn more about Amazon Bedrock.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale. Build with any open source framework and any model. Connect agents to your tools and data with authentication and access controls built in. Monitor and improve agents in production with tracing and evaluation. AgentCore handles the infrastructure so you focus on agent logic, not backend plumbing, and you get enterprise security and reliability without giving up open source flexibility.

Learn more on the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product page.

Why Amazon Bedrock?

Several factors made Amazon Bedrock the ideal choice for Duco’s regulated financial services industry (FSI) environment:

  • Security and compliance first: With Amazon Bedrock, customer data stays within the AWS environment, and it is not used to train models. With private endpoints in its virtual private cloud (VPC), Duco can connect to internal systems while keeping them completely isolated, which matters for sensitive financial data processing.
  • Model flexibility: Access to leading foundation models from the Amazon Nova 2 family, Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Meta, and Mistral AI through a single API means Duco can choose the right model for each task. Duco can switch between models by changing a configuration parameter.
  • Built for financial services: Amazon Bedrock provides the robust governance controls and compliance frameworks that financial services require, avoiding infrastructure complexity while maintaining the security standards tier-one banks demand.

Choosing AgentCore as the runtime

Duco’s existing agent infrastructure was built on LangChain and LangGraph, both of which were already in production. When evaluating runtime options for its agentic workloads, AgentCore emerged as the clear choice for three key reasons:

  • Compatibility with existing primitives: AgentCore is fully compatible with Duco’s existing LangChain and LangGraph code, so most existing code continued to work without modification.
  • Managed runtime: Instead of Duco running its own agent infrastructure, AgentCore provides a fully managed runtime, reducing operational overhead for the engineering team.
  • Regulated environment suitability: AgentCore met the stringent requirements of deploying in regulated financial services environments, with built-in security and compliance controls.

Multi-tenant architecture: Isolation by design

Duco’s platform operates as a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) offering with strict tenant isolation (figure 1). This is a non-negotiable requirement for regulated institutions. The architecture reflects this at every layer, from the underlying cloud infrastructure right up to the AI agent runtime.

Infrastructure layer

  • Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) clusters with namespace-per-tenant isolation and network segregation help maintain workload separation at the Kubernetes layer.
  • Per-tenant dedicated AWS services: every tenant receives a dedicated Amazon Aurora MySQL database, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) storage bucket, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption keys, Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) messaging stack, Amazon ElastiCache layer, and Amazon Cognito user pool. Zero shared data infrastructure across clients.
  • Per-tenant autoscaling helps minimize the impact of one client’s compute-intensive workload on another tenant’s performance.

Security and access control

Isolation is enforced through identity as well as infrastructure, with every hop between the user and their data authenticated (figure 2):

  • Tenant-scoped authentication: every request carries a JSON Web Token (JWT) issued by the tenant’s dedicated Cognito user pool, validated by the inbound authorizer of the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, before agent logic runs.
  • Gateway-mediated tool access: agents reach tools only through the tenant’s dedicated AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which passes calls through to the tenant’s container-based Model Context Protocol (MCP) services running in Amazon EKS.
  • End-to-end user identity: the user’s identity is passed through to downstream services, and each MCP server validates both the agent’s and the user’s identity against the tenant’s Cognito user pool, so every tool call is authorized as the calling user, made by a trusted agent.
  • Private networking: tenants share a VPC and Amazon EKS cluster, segregated by namespace and network policy, with private endpoints keeping traffic to Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore on the AWS network. Each tenant’s AgentCore runtime runs in VPC network mode, with network interfaces in the private subnets, so its outbound traffic enters the VPC and is governed by security groups.

Agent layer

The isolation principle extends fully into the agent architecture:

  • One AgentCore runtime and Gateway per tenant: each tenant is served by a dedicated runtime and Gateway, configured against that tenant’s own Cognito user pool and Amazon EKS namespace. Combined with the built-in session isolation of AgentCore, this means there is no shared memory, context, or tooling between clients. Each bank’s unique schemas, naming conventions, and institutional knowledge remain completely isolated from other tenants.
  • Per-tenant MCP servers: each tenant has its own set of MCP servers providing service-specific capabilities, dynamically discovered at boot time.

The architecture helps maintain a model where each agent only has access to one bank’s data, context, and reasoning, facilitating real isolation of context across banks.

Multi-model strategy

Rather than committing to a single foundation model, Duco uses the right model for each job, assigning each role in its agent design to the model best suited to it. This approach delivers both quality and cost efficiency by matching the right model capability to each specific workload:

ModelPrimary roleUse cases

Anthropic Claude Opus

 Planning agentFor complex reasoning and understanding, formulating up front plans for other agents to execute on
Anthropic Claude SonnetMain reasoning & complex decision-makingException investigation, reconciliation logic, rule interpretation
Anthropic Claude HaikuLightweight tool routing decisionsFast routing choices, low-latency classification, cost-efficient first-pass triage
Amazon Nova 2 ProTool output summarizationCondensing MCP tool responses, generating readable summaries for analysts

This multi-model approach is architecturally designed to allow model swapping without disrupting the stack, which is critical in a landscape where model capabilities evolve rapidly.

Solving context bloat: The MCP skills architecture

One of Duco’s most significant technical innovations addresses a challenge familiar to anyone building production agent systems: context window management.

The problem

With 300–400 tools exposed per tenant through AgentCore Gateway (which fronts a separate MCP server for each underlying Duco service), approximately 200,000 tokens of tool descriptions were loaded into context before work began. This caused context overloading: response quality degraded as conversations lengthened, and the model lost the thread of earlier reasoning. The team emphasized that a feeling an agent is becoming less capable isn’t enough evidence on its own. Evaluations must be run before engineering decisions are made.

The solution: On-demand skills loading

Duco created a skills architecture using MCP resource types to move tool descriptions out of the static context and load them only when needed:

  • skill:// resources
    — on-demand tool descriptions loaded only when a skill is required.
  • system:// resources
    — dynamic system prompt sections composed at runtime, keeping the base system prompt lean.
  • ui:// resources
    — UI-specific resources, isolated from operational tooling.

Three new meta-tools, implemented in Duco’s agent harness, replaced the bloated tool description payload:

  • load_skill
    — fetches skill descriptions on demand, only when the agent determines a skill is needed.
  • find_tool
    — locates relevant tools without loading all schemas into context.
  • invoke_tool
    — executes the selected tool once identified.

The results

  • 90% context reduction: Main context reduced from 200,000 tokens to approximately 20,000 tokens by moving tool descriptions out of static context and limiting the size of tool responses.
  • Prompt caching preserved: the static prompt prefix (system prompt plus the three meta-tools) stays small and stable, and skills load into the conversation rather than the tool list, so loading a skill does not invalidate the cache.
  • Measurably improved agent response quality: validated through a rigorous evaluation framework.
  • Zero infrastructure changes required: same underlying models, same tools, and same tasks, with measurably better outcomes.

MCP tool discovery: Deploy a service, gain a capability

A key architectural decision was implementing MCP tool discovery at boot time. When a new service is deployed, its MCP server is registered as a target on the tenant’s AgentCore Gateway as part of the deployment. When an agent boots, the harness builds a registry of every tool the Gateway exposes and shares just the tool names. The agent then uses find_tool and invoke_tool to discover the details and invoke tools on demand. As a result, the agent automatically gains that capability with no redeployment or agent reconfiguration required. Access control is enforced by the underlying services themselves: because the user’s identity is passed through the Gateway, each tool call succeeds only if that user is permitted to perform the action.

This provides operational agility: the platform team can ship new capabilities to agents by deploying a new microservice, without touching the agent configuration or requiring downtime. For a platform that serves 200+ clients with diverse and evolving operational needs, this dynamic capability model is a significant competitive advantage.

Deploying agents at scale

Duco implemented Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore to power two critical workflows that previously required extensive manual effort:

1. Intelligent onboarding

Previously, onboarding new reconciliation processes was a manual, time-intensive exercise requiring significant professional services resources. Banks would take years to migrate thousands of processes, moving at a pace of roughly one per week.

With Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore, Duco can now:

  • Automatically understand diverse file formats and data structures across legacy and modern systems.
  • Translate legacy configurations from existing systems into structured Duco processes.
  • Parse complex spreadsheet macros written decades ago that no one fully understands.
  • Deploy new reconciliations 10× faster than before.

One global bank experienced a 70% decrease in onboarding costs for new reconciliations and achieved an increase of over 20% in straight-through processing through better match rates and allocation rules.

2. AI-driven exception investigation

Financial institutions run thousands of quality gates between systems, generating countless exceptions daily. Traditionally, armies of analysts manually investigate each break to determine if it’s worth worrying about, already being investigated, or represents a new risk.

Duco’s agents now handle the “first mile” of investigation:

  • Triage new breaks as they arrive, grouping related exceptions that share a likely root cause.
  • Check context, such as whether a break is already known, already being worked, or a timing difference expected to clear.
  • Investigate by pulling evidence from source data and systems to trace the root cause of each inconsistency, whether a data quality issue, a missing or late record, a mapping or reference data problem, or a genuine mismatch, and explain why it happened.
  • Recommend a decision-ready case: the likely cause, a proposed resolution such as an adjustment, a rule change, or an escalation, the alternatives considered, and the supporting evidence.
  • Route each case to the right analyst, who reviews the evidence and makes the final call, with every decision recorded in the audit trail.

This agentic approach excels because financial workflows involve highly variable paths through information, exactly the kind of complex, context-heavy reasoning that foundation models handle well.

Operating in a regulated environment

Deploying AI agents in financial services requires more than technical capability. It demands rigorous compliance, auditability, and risk management. Duco’s implementation on Amazon Bedrock addresses these requirements through four core principles:

  • Comprehensive observability: Every agent decision is logged in a complete audit trail. Reviewers can trace each decision to check it against regulatory requirements.
  • Human-in-the-loop controls: High-risk actions require explicit authorization, with clear escalation pathways for complex scenarios that exceed agent confidence thresholds.
  • Fail-safe architecture: Systems default to client protection over operational efficiency, supporting safety even when agents encounter edge cases or unexpected data.
  • Regulatory alignment: The platform supports workloads subject to SOC 2 and DORA requirements, with data residency controls per institution.

Results that matter

Duco’s adoption of Amazon Bedrock has delivered measurable, auditable business impact across client deployments:

10×

Faster reconciliation deployments

70%

Reduction in onboarding costs

20%+

Increase in straight-through processing

1000s

Hours saved in manual investigation

Perhaps most importantly, Duco now has a foundation for rapid innovation. Building new agentic capabilities no longer requires extensive machine learning engineering, so the team can focus on solving business problems rather than managing infrastructure.

Roadmap: The future of human–agent collaboration

Duco’s architecture is designed not to replace workers, but to elevate them. The platform envisions a clear progression in human roles as agentic capabilities mature:

Task Worker → Investigator → Decision Maker

Rather than humans performing repetitive tasks, the future sees operations teams orchestrating multiple agents in parallel with humans making final approval decisions based on agent-prepared analysis. The architecture is designed to support agent-to-agent communication, including cross-firm scenarios where agents at different financial institutions could coordinate.

Conclusion

For regulated financial institutions, Duco’s architecture shows that agentic AI isn’t only viable. It’s already delivering at production scale. Duco rebuilt its agentic AI stack on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining strict per-tenant isolation, the right model for each job, and an MCP skills architecture that cut context overhead by 90%. The results include reconciliation deployments 10× faster and, for one global bank, onboarding costs down 70% and straight-through processing up by over 20%. To build a similar multi-tenant setup, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide, then read Building multi-tenant agents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore on the AWS Machine Learning Blog. For the operating model behind this work, see Duco’s Agentic Operations: a new operating model for post-trade.

entries.title: Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing
entries.summary: Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, not a model problem. This post gives a field-tested taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns and anti-patterns, a framework for deciding when multiple agents are warranted, and how to build cost-efficient, reliable systems on AWS.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Taxonomy of multi-agent design patterns, anti-patterns, and lessons from manufacturing

Enterprise teams are building multi-agent systems, and when early implementations fall short, the cause is rarely the model. Multi-agent coordination is a distributed systems problem, and many teams taking it on haven’t yet built distributed systems instincts.

The numbers are consistent across sources: ~88% of AI pilots never reach production. Stanford HAI demonstrated that two models can perform worse collaborating than either alone when coordination overhead exceeds the benefit. The pattern is clear: teams are adding complexity faster than they build understanding. Ten steps that are each 95 percent reliable deliver only 59.9 percent end-to-end reliability, and 20 steps deliver 35.8 percent. This illustrative model assumes a strictly sequential chain with no retries, but the direction holds: each dependent handoff multiplies risk.

In this post, you learn how to decide whether a use case needs multiple agents, choose a coordination pattern, and spot costly anti-patterns early. You also see how takt time, safety boundaries, edge data, and shift cycles shape the architecture.

Multi-agent coordination patterns

Coordination patterns fall into two tiers, based on who controls the flow. In Tier 1, you define the path.

In Tier 2, the model chooses the path at runtime. That flexibility handles work whose steps you can’t define in advance, at a higher cost in tokens, latency, and debugging. The practical default is to start with Tier 1 and move a task to Tier 2 only when its subtasks emerge during the work.

Tier 1: Patterns (deterministic control flow)

1.1 Sequential Pipeline: Orchestration patterns that implement linear execution where each node’s output feeds into the next node (A -> B -> C) supporting ordered processing with predictable execution timing

In the following diagram, input flows to agent A (extract), then agent B (transform), then agent C (validate), and then output. The user defines that order at build time, and nothing is decided at runtime. As a result, the pipeline is straightforward to debug and test, and its cost is predictable. Typical fits include document processing, extract, transform, and load (ETL) chains, and warranty-claim triage.

1.2 Conditional Workflow: Logic-based edges select the next node by condition, so the workflow can branch and send each case down a different path.

In the following diagram, a user request goes to agent A (write code) and then to agent B (test code). A pass/fail check sends passing work to agent D (deploy). Failing work loops back to agent A for a retry, up to a maximum of N times, and then escalates to a human. The orchestration layer enforces that cap, for example through an AWS Step Functions iteration limit, which keeps the loop from becoming the unbounded iteration anti-pattern described later in this post.

1.3 Conditional Router:

A classification step examines the input and directs it to the appropriate processing path. Only one path is executed per request. Best for intent-driven dispatch, quality-gate decisions, customer inquiry routing, and anomaly triage.

The following diagram shows a plant supervisor’s request being read by a classifier and sent to exactly one specialist. Questions about whether parts meet spec go to the Quality Agent, overdue equipment services go to the Maintenance Agent, and shift changes go to the Scheduling Agent. This decision is made at the entry point.

1.4 Parallel Workflow: A task splits into independent subtasks that run simultaneously across handlers, each on its own data. A fan-in step combines the results when all handlers complete, and a failure in one path retries only that path. Best for multi-source analysis, batch processing, and work that decomposes into independent pieces.

In the following diagram, a research orchestrator decomposes the task and dispatches it to three specialist agents that run concurrently: a financial data agent, a geopolitical agent, and a logistics agent, each analyzing its own source. A combined step waits for all three, then synthesizes the results, resolves conflicts, and ranks the findings. Latency equals the slowest single agent rather than the sum of all three.

Tier 2: Autonomous patterns (LLM-determined control flow)

In autonomous patterns, control flow is determined at runtime by the AI model itself, not predefined by developers. Agents read task state, reason about what’s needed and coordinate through shared context rather than fixed paths spanning a spectrum from structured orchestration to fully emergent behavior.

2.1 Plan-based orchestration

In plan-based orchestration, a single orchestrator agent acts as a project manager. The orchestrator maintains an explicit task plan with assignments and dependencies, sees all context while each worker receives only its slice, distributes work dynamically against the current plan, and monitors progress centrally. Key design choice is that the workers are stateless and independent. If one fails, it doesn’t contaminate others. The orchestrator retries only the failed worker, not the entire workflow.

The following diagram shows how a planner agent decomposes a task into an explicit plan and dispatches each step to a worker’s agent. Each step goes to a dedicated worker (a research agent, an analysis agent, and a report agent) that sees only its assigned slice.

2.2 Handoff pattern

Agents operate with limited, local knowledge and coordinate through peer-to-peer delegation. Each makes local decisions about when and to whom to transfer control, based on the task and the agents it knows. Control passes with state: each transfer carries validated task state, the evidence behind it, and any unresolved questions, so the receiving agent continues rather than reinterpreting a summary. A handoff that moves only through the conversation is not a handoff.

In the following diagram, a customer service agent transfers control, together with its context, to either a technical support agent or a billing agent, and technical support can hand off further to a senior engineer. Each agent knows only the small set of peers it can transfer to.

2.3 Conversation-driven pattern

In conversation-driven patterns (also known as group chat patterns), all agents participate in a shared conversation where orchestration emerges through turn-taking rather than explicit plans or structured handoffs. This mirrors human team collaboration where everyone can see the discussion and contribute when appropriate.

In the following diagram, an agent-selection mechanism decides whose turn it is, and agents A, B, and C each add to one shared conversation, where every turn is a message plus a tool call. The selection mechanism sets the turn-taking, and state lives implicitly in the conversation history.

Control flow characteristics:

  • Visibility: Broadcast all agents observe all messages in the shared conversation.
  • Decision making: Next speaker selected based on conversation context, not predetermined plans.
  • State management: Implicit in the conversation history.
  • Turn-taking: Determined by selection mechanisms (round-robin, AI-driven)
    • Round-robin. Agents take turns in a fixed, repeating order until a termination condition is met, which keeps it predictable.
    • AI-driven. A model selects the next speaker from the conversation context rather than a fixed order.

2.4 Debate/consensus

Multiple agents independently evaluate the same input, and their conclusions are reconciled by majority, by a judge agent, or by escalation when they disagree. Unlike a conversation-driven pattern, the agents do not see each other’s reasoning before committing to a position, which is what makes disagreement informative rather than socially convergent.

Use it sparingly. Debate is the most expensive pattern here, and on perceptual tasks it buys latency rather than accuracy (see the quality-inspection case in anti-pattern 3 that follows). Reserve it for high-stakes, low-volume decisions where being wrong costs more than deliberating.

Hybrid approaches

In practice, most production systems combine several patterns based on task decomposition:

  • Use workflow patterns for predictable, well-understood components.
  • Apply autonomous patterns where flexibility and adaptation are essential.
  • Implement task management patterns (termination, delegation) consistently across all orchestration types.
  • Design hierarchical compositions where complex agents internally use different patterns at different layers.

The governing principle: pattern-to-task alignment. Match the orchestration approach to each task’s inherent characteristics and your system’s reliability requirements rather than forcing everything through a single pattern.

Anti-patterns that burn budget

Each of the following five anti-patterns looks reasonable at design time, and each surfaces later as an inflated token cost, a missed takt-time window, or a decision that has quietly drifted out of sync with the plant floor.

1. God agent

One agent owns overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) analysis, programmable logic controller (PLC) diagnostics, and maintenance behind a single prompt with 15 or more tools. Tool selection degrades as tools grow, and failures become hard to attribute.

The fix: Bounded agents of five tools or fewer, such as an OEE analyst, a fault diagnostician, and a maintenance drafter.

2. Unbounded iteration

The agent loops on “try again” with no hard stop. A four-agent system can burn a significantly higher number of tokens before a single retry, and no one call trips an alarm. Retries multiply coordination failures rather than fixing them.

The fix: Hard iteration ceiling in code, per-agent token ceiling, budget alarm wired to an automatic stop. Infrastructure enforces limits. The model will not stop itself.

3. Natural-language contracts

Agents hand each other free-text prose with no schema. Interpretation hardens at every hop: “could indicate wear” becomes “confirmed wear” becomes a maintenance order. The drift happens between agents, where tracing is thinnest.

4. Premature multi-agent

Multi-agent where one agent with tool groups would do. Each agent adds a coordination tax that is not linear, and the gains flatten around four. Most “specialists” are one model in different costumes.

The fix: Needs at least two different models, different tool access, concurrent execution, and real interdependency. Fewer than two, and one agent with action groups does it.

The test: can one agent handle the phases by switching tools? Then it is not a multi-agent problem.

5. Unguarded customer contact

The agent triggers real-world actions (email, service visits, machine parameters) with no approval step. Hallucinations cross into the physical world, irreversible actions compound, and liability escalates from a refund to product liability.

The fix: Defense in depth: recommendation → Amazon Bedrock Guardrails → schema validation → business rules → human approval → execution.

Every point where agent output reaches a customer, or a safety system is a trust boundary.

Choosing an architecture

With the patterns and anti-patterns in view, the architecture choice comes down to a short sequence of questions.

  • Does the task require action beyond text generation? Treat a direct model call as the baseline and add orchestration only for a measured reason. Summarizing documents or generating code from a specification rarely supplies one.
  • Is the solution path known in advance? If you can write down what happens in what order, you don’t have a “how many agents” decision at all. Your real choice is simpler: a single agent that calls tools, or a Tier 1 workflow.
  • Does the work require genuinely distinct expertise? Separate domains with established handoffs justify specialized agents. A single domain belongs to one agent, no matter how many tools it needs.
  • Does the solution emerge only through exploration? When the action sequence is known and can run as an act-and-validate loop, it belongs to a single agent, even one that plans its steps dynamically. Tier 2 earns its added cost, latency, and debugging burden only when the subtasks themselves are discovered in the course of the work.

The following decision tree turns these four questions into a path you can follow from top to bottom.

The tree starts by asking whether the task requires actions beyond text generation. If it doesn’t, a simple model call is enough. If it does, the tree asks whether the solution is well known and can be expressed as a workflow. On the known solution side, work that benefits from specialized expertise or domain separation go to a Tier 1 multi-agent workflow (a pipeline, fan-out, or router). Everything else goes to a single agent with tools and action groups. On the unknown-solution side, only tasks that involve exploration or significant side effects go to Tier 2 for autonomous multi-agent patterns. The rest stays with a single agent. The guiding principle is to choose the simplest architecture that meets your requirements.

The following chart compares the patterns on four things: when to reach for each one, how control flows between agents, how deterministic the result is, and what it costs to build and operate. Build cost is a relative scale, not an estimate.

Tier 1 patterns score high on determinism at low to moderate build cost. Tier 2 patterns give more of the path to the model, and plan-based orchestration costs the most to build. If you can draw the control flow on a whiteboard before runtime, start with Tier 1.

Applied: Mapping patterns to manufacturing use cases

Use CasePatternRationale
Shift handoff summarizationSequential PipelineLinear: raw logs → summary → report
Multi-station root-cause analysisPlan-Based OrchestratorDynamic: subtasks discovered during analysis
Real-time quality gateConditional Router + Edge AgentIn-cycle: local model decides. Agent reasoning off path
Predictive maintenance schedulingParallel Fan-Out/Fan-InIndependent models per asset class
Engineering change order impactDebate/ConsensusHigh stakes: adversarial review justified
Supplier communication draftingSequential + Human GateMust not auto-send (see Unguarded Customer Contact)
Cross-plant optimizationPlan-Based OrchestratorMulti-source: dynamic queries. Solver does allocation

The manufacturing lens: Four constraints that change the calculus

Manufacturing is not a generic enterprise IT environment, and four constraints make that arithmetic unforgiving.

Constraint 1: Production-line latency = direct revenue loss

Automotive body shops, where robots weld the vehicle body together, typically run at 60 jobs per hour. Each of their over 40 stations has a 60-second takt time before the line advances. Inference latency that sits on a station’s cycle path eats into those 60 seconds, and a delay at the bottleneck station slows the whole line. Even a 2 percent throughput reduction can translate to significant annual revenue impact.

Architecture implication: budget latency at p99, not average. The tail is what stops the line. Give every agent a sub-second deterministic fallback, and match it to the risk:

  • Advisory/quality-flagging: Pass the part with a flag for end-of-line review.
  • Safety-critical: Containment or a deterministic stop, not continuation.
  • Decide this mapping per station before deployment.

Constraint 2: Safety has physical consequences

A hallucinated chatbot causes embarrassment. A hallucinated welding parameter causes structural defects that surface in crash testing or field failure and can lead to a safety recall. Two failure modes recur:

  • OT/IT boundary state desync: An agent reads the manufacturing execution system (MES) as Station 12 running Part #A, but a manual PLC override already switched it to Part #B, so it tunes parameters for the wrong part.
  • Hallucinated safety boundary: A maintenance agent reasons about lockout/tagout from scratch and declares Station 7 accessible while adjacent Station 6 runs, breaking the interlock zone.

Architecture implication:

The boundary: keep the deterministic core unchanged, including PLCs, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, and the MES, and wrap an advisory layer around it.

  • Agents observe, analyze, and recommend. They do not actuate.
  • Safety constraints live as deterministic guardrails in an external service that agents query rather than reason about. They’re never embedded in prompts, where they can be argued away.

Validation and approval: A recommendation passes schema validation and physics simulation, checked against the OT source of truth immediately before actuation, never against OT state cached beyond one cycle. It’s then approved at a level matched to its scope:

  • Level 0: Agent resolves autonomously.
  • Level 1: Operator confirms with one click.
  • Level 2: Engineer decides from the presented analysis.
  • Level 3: Management evaluates a line-stop recommendation.

Only then does a validated command interface pass permitted commands to deterministic control. The large language model (LLM) proposes. The physics engine and the human operator dispose.

Constraint 3: Data lives at the edge

A single stamping press generates 50+ GB/day of sensor data whose value decays in milliseconds. Shipping it to the cloud costs more in bandwidth than compute, and by the time the cloud answers, the press has moved on.

Architecture implication: hybrid edge-cloud is the practical default, and the Constraint 2 boundary holds at the edge too.

  • Edge (AWS IoT Greengrass): sub-takt anomaly detection, threshold monitoring, and stop-or-continue signals at the source: the edge agent recommends, the PLC acts.
  • Cloud: What the edge can’t do: cross-shift analytics, trend correlation across plants, and model retraining on fleet data. The edge distills and transmits only what matters.

Constraint 4: Shift-aligned agent lifecycle

Unbounded context makes an agent drift as stale observations crowd out current reality. A full reset loses continuity between shifts. Manufacturing already solves this for humans with structured shift handoffs, and agents need the same discipline.

Architecture implication: Bound agent memory to the shift cycle.

  • Initialize: Shift context, including the crew roster, production targets, and the prior shift handoff.
  • Accumulate: Working memory within the shift window only.
  • Hand off: Emit a shift-end summary of open issues, flagged anomalies, and recommendations that seed the next crew, mirroring the human ritual without unbounded context growth.

Building on AWS

The following managed services map to the concerns raised earlier in this post. Each row names the mechanism, not just the service.

NeedServiceMechanism
RuntimeAgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Where agents run, their control flow is determined or model determined. Bring Strands, LangGraph, or CrewAI.
Shift-bounded memoryAgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Managed short-term and long-term context, so the shift-scoped memory from Constraint 4 is configuration rather than custom state plumbing.
Typed handoffsAgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Converts APIs and AWS Lambda functions into Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools with validated schemas, so handoffs carry typed fields rather than prose.
Agent permissionsAgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore A unique, verifiable identity for each agent with fine-grained access control. It’s the enforcement point for which agent can reach which system, and on whose behalf.
Tracing between agentsAgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Spans and traces across runtime, memory, gateway, and tools, through Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search and AWS Distro for Open Telemetry (ADOT). Handoffs are the least observable part of a multi-agent system and where untyped contracts fail silently.
Human approval surfaceAWS Quick Where the escalation tiers land. AWS Quick Automate runs approval workflows with one-click approval in Slack, and its action connectors can invoke Amazon Bedrock AgentCore agents.
Tiered model selectionAmazon Bedrock One API across model families, so cost tiering is configuration: a small model for a router’s classification and a stronger one for an orchestrator synthesis.

Conclusion

Multi-agent systems change how automotive manufacturers orchestrate intelligence at scale, but only when built on the right foundations.

The patterns and anti-patterns here come from real deployments where poor architecture shows up as runaway token costs, takt-time violations, and, at worst, physical safety risks. The economics at plant scale are unforgiving, because token volume grows with every agent, robot, and shift. Tiered model selection, context compression, and edge-cloud distribution are the main levers for delivering the same value at a fraction of that cost.

The recommendation here is to start with Tier 1 patterns, prove value, and then expand. Most manufacturing use cases, such as shift handoff summarization, quality-gate decisions, and predictive maintenance, are well served by deterministic workflows. Reserve autonomous orchestration for genuinely open-ended problems where dynamic subtask discovery justifies the added cost, latency, and debugging complexity.

entries.title: How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of AI agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that let marketing and product teams draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation. Learn how MoEngage turned its existing APIs into MCP tools and kept each tenant's data isolated while giving agents secure access to live platform data.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How MoEngage built agentic customer engagement on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

This post was co-written with Ashwin Srinivasan, Nishan Das and Karthik Baile from MoEngage.

A marketing or product team member planning a weekend flash sale often opens three tools before writing a single line of copy. First they open the analytics dashboard to see what worked last time, then the content library to find the right tone, and then the campaign builder to build the campaign itself. Repeat that across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp, and much of a marketing team’s week goes to navigating tools instead of making decisions.

The MoEngage Model Context Protocol (MCP) Connector gives an MCP-compatible assistant, such as Claude or ChatGPT, secure, tenant-scoped access to a brand’s segments, campaign history, and content library.

This capability points to a broader shift in software platforms. Beyond a user interface for business users and an API for engineering teams, a third layer is emerging, where a user describes an outcome in plain language and an agent carries out the steps across the platform. For a customer engagement platform, that means a capability already exposed as an API can become a tool an agent calls, and a campaign that once moved across several tools can move through one conversation instead.

MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use across channels including push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and Rich Communication Services (RCS), set out to build this layer. MoEngage built Merlin AI, a set of artificial intelligence (AI) agents that work with live platform data. Marketing and product teams can now draft, analyze, and adjust campaigns from a single conversation, while agents decide what to send each customer. One customer, Glance, saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates as a result.

MoEngage treated this as an architecture problem. The question was how to give agents secure, tenant-scoped access to live data without rebuilding hundreds of existing APIs. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage solved it with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize AI agents at scale with any framework or model. The post covers the four agent modes in Merlin AI, how MoEngage exposed its existing APIs as MCP tools, and how the architecture keeps each tenant’s data isolated. It closes with the results MoEngage customers have seen and the pattern other software providers can reuse.

Solution overview: Four agent modes in Merlin AI

Merlin AI runs four kinds of agents. All four share the same foundation: foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for reasoning and generation, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for hosting, and MCP for standardized access to data. Across all four modes, Merlin AI uses Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock for reasoning, tool-call planning, and content generation. For the full list of models, see Supported foundation models in Amazon Bedrock.

Embedded agents in Merlin AI Studio

Merlin AI Studio places purpose-built agents at the exact point in the workflow where marketing and product teams do that piece of work:

  • Copywriter generates personalized push and transactional copy that stays consistent with the brand voice.
  • Designer produces a marketing banner or image from a text description.
  • Segment Assist turns a plain-language audience description into the correct set of attributes and filters. For example, a marketing or product team member can ask for users who abandoned a cart in the last 2 hours.
  • Jinja Assist converts natural-language requests into working Jinja and Liquid markup for dynamic content.
  • In-app Template Builder creates responsive, accessible HTML templates for in-app messages, including gamified formats, lead-capture pop-ups, and surveys.
  • Flow Assist turns a high-level idea into a ready-to-deploy customer journey. Behind the scenes, a sequence of specialized steps interprets the request, proposes paths, builds the flow structure, refines it with historical data, and packages it for deployment.

Conversational agents

Conversational agents work across campaigns, analytics, segments, and flows. A user can ask a question in plain language and the agent calls the right tools to answer it or act on it. The Campaign Insights Agent, embedded on the analytics page, delegates to specialized sub-agents. One sub-agent runs analysis across several metrics at once. A second diagnoses why a metric is underperforming, and a third compares performance across time periods or segments. A final step formats the findings into a clear answer.

Custom agents

Custom agents let lifecycle and customer relationship management (CRM) teams design agents that run continuously on MoEngage data and tools, inside rules the product and marketing team defines. Every agent shows its work through an activity log of the data it pulled, the decisions it made, the channels it touched, and the content it sent. Teams can run an agent with full autonomy or require human review before anything executes.

Decisioning agents

Decisioning agents act for each individual customer. Each agent decides what to say, when, how often, and on which channel, and it learns from every outcome. Product and marketing teams set the content, goals, and guardrails, and the agents handle the rest, with visibility into every decision. Offer Decisioning selects the best offer on web and app surfaces. Campaign Decisioning delivers 1:1 decisions across email, push, SMS, and WhatsApp. Together with workflow agents, this puts both halves of agentic marketing in one system.

Architecture overview

The architecture has four layers. Each layer has a single responsibility and can change without affecting the others.

  • Clients. Merlin AI agents inside the MoEngage product, and external MCP clients such as Claude and ChatGPT, through the MoEngage MCP Connector, connect to the MoEngage MCP server. Clients that support MCP can connect.
  • MCP server on AgentCore runtime. MoEngage hosts its MCP server on AgentCore runtime. The server exposes MoEngage platform capabilities as MCP tools. It does not run its own model. Reasoning happens in the agent that calls it.
  • MoEngage platform APIs. The MCP server calls the same OpenAPI 3.0-compatible APIs that MoEngage customers already use. These APIs enforce existing permissions and data residency rules.
  • Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock. Agents use foundation models in Amazon Bedrock to plan tool calls, generate content, and summarize results. For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

In a typical request, a user signs in to MoEngage and asks a question. The client sends the request with the user’s existing JSON Web Token (JWT). AgentCore runtime validates the token and starts an isolated session for that user. The agent asks a model in Amazon Bedrock which tools to call. The MCP server calls the MoEngage APIs with the user’s tenant context and returns the results. The agent then composes the answer.

The following diagram shows how these components connect.

Turning existing APIs into MCP tools

MoEngage opens its platform to agents through an MCP server and agent-callable APIs. Its platform APIs for campaigns, analytics, segments, content, and flows were already OpenAPI 3.0-compatible, so MoEngage used the FastMCP framework to generate MCP tools from those specifications. Each operation becomes a tool with a structured schema, a description, and parameter validation.

The following simplified example shows the pattern:

The tools fall into five groups:

  • Campaign tools create, edit, schedule, and send campaigns across channels.
  • Analytics tools query delivery funnels, click-through rates, conversions, and cohort performance.
  • Segmentation tools list, inspect, and create segments from behavioral and attribute filters.
  • Content tools manage content blocks, templates, and dynamic content rules.
  • Flow tools inspect, pause, or modify automation journeys.

The tools come from the specifications, so they stay in sync with the APIs. When a team updates a specification, the tool definitions update with it.

Keeping tenants isolated and identity out of the model’s reach

A multi-tenant system cannot let a model decide whose data it is reading. MoEngage made three design choices to help prevent that. First, the MCP server reuses the existing authentication model, accepting the same JWT-based authentication that MoEngage APIs already use, and AgentCore runtime validates each token before a request reaches the server. Second, workspace and user context travel in request headers that AgentCore runtime forwards to the server rather than as tool arguments, so the model does not see these values and cannot change them. Third, AgentCore runtime runs each user session in its own isolated environment, so one user’s conversation cannot read another’s session state.

On top of this, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails apply content safety and personally identifiable information (PII) filters to agent responses. A backend-for-frontend layer then validates the structure of generated content before the MoEngage interface renders it.

Give users control over agents. Users set guardrails on what each agent can do, review every action in its activity log, and choose between autonomous and human-reviewed execution.

Why MoEngage chose AgentCore runtime

AgentCore runtime provides the production capabilities that a multi-tenant MCP server needs, and each one addresses a specific requirement of MoEngage’s workload. AgentCore runtime scales sessions as demand changes, so MoEngage does not plan capacity for traffic bursts across its customer workspaces. Each session runs in its own isolated environment by default, which keeps one brand’s conversation and data separate from another’s. The built-in JWT authorizer validates tokens against MoEngage’s existing identity provider, so the MCP server uses the same authentication model as the APIs.

Hosting on AgentCore runtime is also framework-agnostic. MoEngage can change models or agent frameworks without touching the MCP server, which matters as the agent layer evolves. Built-in metrics, logs, and traces through Amazon CloudWatch give MoEngage engineers visibility into every session. Together, these capabilities let the team focus on agent logic and marketing intelligence rather than hosting infrastructure.

Inference through Amazon Bedrock gave MoEngage two more benefits. Merlin AI agents run on Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 on Amazon Bedrock, and MoEngage moves between these versions through the same Amazon Bedrock API. MoEngage also pays per token instead of operating GPU infrastructure. Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train foundation models, which matters for a system that processes customer engagement data at scale.

One campaign, one conversation

The following example shows how a user builds a campaign without leaving the conversation.

  • Ask for the draft. The user types:

    Draft a weekend flash sale push for our high-value segment, using the same tone as our best-performing December campaign.

    The agent calls the analytics tools to find the top December campaign, the segmentation tools to confirm the high-value segment, and the content tools to pull the brand voice. It returns a draft with several copy variants.
