  • Check what underperformed. The user asks:

    Which push notifications last month had below 2% click-through rate (CTR), and what do they have in common?

    The Campaign Insights Agent compares those campaigns and reports the shared pattern, such as send time or audience overlap.

  • Adjust the journey. The user asks:

    Show me the drop-off at step 3 of our onboarding flow, and pause the SMS branch if it’s below 5% conversion.

    The agent reads the flow state through the flow tools and pauses the branch after the user confirms. This is the human-review mode in practice.

Each step uses the same tools that power the MoEngage interface. The user does not open a separate dashboard.

Results

Merlin AI agents on this architecture have been in production for more than 6 months. One customer, Glance, reached campaign go-live 50% faster and saw a 38% uplift in push notification click-through rates. With Merlin AI Copywriter, Glance teams also produce about three times more content variants per campaign.

Across the platform, MoEngage reports a 60–70% reduction in manual effort by marketing and product teams for channel, timing, and frequency decisions, and a 20–30% improvement in conversion rates from goal-based decisioning. Managed, pay-per-token inference in Amazon Bedrock reduced AI infrastructure costs by more than 50% compared with self-hosted models.

AgentCore feature availability varies by AWS Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation.

Conclusion

MoEngage made its platform agent-ready without rebuilding it. Existing OpenAPI specifications became MCP tools. AgentCore runtime provided hosting, authentication, and session isolation. Foundation models in Amazon Bedrock provided reasoning and generation. The result is a platform where marketing and product teams move from question to action in one conversation, where MoEngage engineers spend their time on marketing intelligence rather than infrastructure, and where agents handle workflows for the team and decisions for every customer while users stay in control.

The same pattern applies to other software providers with a mature API surface. Start from your existing specifications, keep identity outside the model, and let a managed runtime handle the production concerns.

To build your own MCP server on the same foundation, start with the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation and follow the AgentCore runtime guide to host it. To choose a foundation model for your agents and review the security and data-handling controls, see the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. To generate MCP tools from your existing OpenAPI specifications, review the FastMCP documentation. To see Merlin AI in action, visit MoEngage Merlin AI. To plan a similar architecture, contact your AWS account team or Solutions Architect.

entries.title: Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform
entries.summary: Legacy mainframe Assembler applications are costly to maintain and hard to staff. This post presents a multi-stage, AI-powered methodology using Amazon Bedrock, Kiro IDE, and AWS Transform to extract business rules, convert Assembler through an intermediate COBOL stage, and deploy modernized Java Spring Boot applications on AWS.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Modernizing mainframe Assembler to Java using Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform

Imagine a batch job that has run every night for decades without failing, and the only person who understands its code is about to retire. We have seen this situation again and again while working with banking, insurance, and airline customers. Their Assembler programs still run critical business operations, but fewer people can read them each year. Rewriting them by hand takes years, risks breaking business rules nobody remembers writing, and still depends on the same experts who are leaving. Amazon Bedrock and AWS Transform change that equation.

This post shows you a multi-stage transformation methodology using Amazon Bedrock, Kiro IDE (an AI-powered integrated development environment), and AWS Transform that can help reduce modernization time compared to manual approaches while maintaining business logic integrity through validation checkpoints. You will learn how to systematically extract business rules from Assembler code, convert them through an intermediate COBOL stage, and deploy modernized applications as Java Spring Boot services on AWS.

Prerequisites

Before starting the modernization process, make sure you have:

  • Active AWS account with least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for Amazon Bedrock, AWS Transform, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
  • Access to Amazon Q Developer or Kiro for AI-assisted code analysis.
  • Access to AWS Transform for COBOL to Java conversion.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock with appropriate foundation models (FMs).
  • An Amazon S3 bucket configured for source code and artifact storage, with encryption and Block Public Access enabled.
  • Knowledge of the target business domain and application functionality.
  • Availability of business and technical subject matter experts (SMEs) for validation sessions.
  • Source Assembler code inventory with available documentation.
  • Test data sets with expected outputs for functional equivalence testing.

Solution overview

You can transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications tightly bounded with COBOL into Java Spring Boot applications built for the AWS cloud through a systematic five-phase approach. This multi-stage methodology, converting Assembler to COBOL as an intermediate step before Java transformation, reduces risk and preserves business logic with greater reliability than direct Assembler-to-Java conversion. The intermediate COBOL stage provides a structured, human-readable format that subject matter experts (SMEs) can validate before final transformation. This makes sure that business rules remain intact throughout the modernization journey. The following sections describe both the current mainframe architecture and the target cloud-focused state.

Current state

Your current architecture represents a traditional mainframe environment where Assembler programs execute batch processes, connected with COBOL, interact with databases, and process files. At its core, JCL (Job Control Language) jobs trigger Assembler program execution at scheduled intervals. These programs read input from VSAM (Virtual Storage Access Method) and sequential files and perform operations against IBM Db2 for z/OS. Your business logic executes using low-level register operations (direct CPU register manipulation) and memory management. Output is written back to files or database tables, and job completion status is reported through JCL return codes. All of this runs on IBM z/OS mainframe infrastructure.

Target state

The modernization solution helps you transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the AWS cloud through a multi-phase, AI-powered workflow. The architecture uses Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for AI-assisted code analysis and business rule extraction, and AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion.

If COBOL source code is already available, you follow the conventional approach and provide it directly to AWS Transform for conversion to Java Spring Boot applications.

With this solution, you can achieve:

  • Reduced transformation time compared to manual approaches.
  • Systematic business logic preservation through validation checkpoints.
  • Human-in-the-loop validation at critical stages.
  • Automated code conversion with functional equivalence testing.

You begin the transformation workflow by analyzing Assembler code to generate Business Rules Extraction (BRE) documentation. You then create detailed functional specifications with human-in-the-loop refinement. The validated specifications guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, generating intermediate COBOL code that bridges the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs. This COBOL code undergoes functional equivalence testing before AWS Transform converts it to Java, with validation checkpoints at each phase to reduce risk and verify business continuity.

Business rules extraction with AI

The quality of your Business Rules Extraction (BRE) directly impacts transformation accuracy, so focus carefully on this phase. Use Amazon Bedrock, through Kiro IDE or the Amazon Bedrock console, along with AWS Transform for mainframe to extract and document business rules from your Assembler source code.

You can use the prompts in this post directly in Amazon Bedrock through the Chat Playground, or within Kiro IDE using its built-in AI chat and Spec panel. Replace the placeholder values with your actual Assembler code and context before running.

Amazon Bedrock is the inference platform behind the first four phases: business rules extraction, specification creation, Assembler-to-COBOL conversion, and validation. Choose a foundation model with strong code reasoning and a large context window, because Assembler programs are long and dense. Set the temperature to 0 so you get consistent output across runs. To process many programs, call the same prompts through the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and store each output in your Amazon S3 bucket so it can feed the next phase. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use your prompts or model outputs to train AWS models or share them with third parties. For details, see Data protection in Amazon Bedrock. Use sanitized test data instead of production data or personally identifiable information (PII).

The more context you provide to the AI, the better it understands the business intent behind the code. Include relevant documentation, data dictionaries, and available business context alongside the Assembler code when prompting.

Note: Save the output of each prompt as you go. You will need them as inputs in the next phase.

Example prompt for context-aware analysis:

You can customize this prompt by adding domain-specific terminology from your business context. When you run this prompt, you will see structured JSON output that you can use for automated validation and direct integration with downstream transformation tools. Data mapping accuracy directly affects conversion quality. Incomplete mappings can lead to lost or corrupted business logic.

Validate with SMEs

Treat AI-generated BRE documents as drafts, not final outputs. Have subject matter experts review and validate the extracted rules before moving forward. Document discrepancies in a validation log and update the BRE based on SME feedback before proceeding to specification creation.

To help SMEs validate the rules, supplement textual BRE documents with visual aids like flowcharts and data flow diagrams. Maintain a validation checklist covering business rule accuracy, data mapping correctness, edge case handling, and error condition completeness.

Extracting spec-driven data flow

After you validate business rules with SMEs, translate them into detailed functional specifications that will guide code conversion. This spec-driven approach confirms that business requirements are clearly documented and agreed upon before code transformation begins, reducing costly rework later.

Use the extracted BRE documents to create complete functional specifications that guide COBOL code generation. These specifications should include program overview, COBOL data structures, process flow design, and business rules coverage mapping.

Example prompt for functional specification generation:

You can adjust the data structure specifications based on your COBOL standards. When you run this prompt, you will receive a complete functional specification with full traceability from business rules to COBOL structures, ready for SME review and direct integration with Kiro for code generation.

Converting legacy Assembler to COBOL

With validated functional specifications in hand, the next phase uses these structured outputs to guide the Assembler-to-COBOL conversion. The intermediate COBOL step helps you bridge the gap between low-level hardware instructions and business-oriented constructs, which helps you verify that business logic is preserved before the final Java transformation.

Example prompt to guide the conversion:

You can modify the formatting requirements to match your organization’s COBOL standards. When you run this prompt, you will generate COBOL code designed to be syntactically correct, logically equivalent to the original Assembler, and fully traceable, with comments linking each code section back to specific business rules from the BRE document. Once generated, rigorously validate the COBOL code before proceeding to the final Java transformation.

Validating the transformation

You should treat testing as an ongoing activity throughout the transformation process, not only a final phase. Your functional equivalence validation between Assembler and COBOL code should employ a comprehensive testing framework that systematically evaluates syntax correctness, structural alignment, logic equivalence, data flow integrity, business rules coverage, and specification compliance.

Example prompt to guide the testing:

You can customize the validation thresholds based on your quality requirements. When you run this prompt, you will receive a comprehensive validation report with actionable recommendations for addressing gaps in program structure, conditional logic, data transformations, and traceability between the original Assembler instructions and the modernized COBOL implementation.

COBOL to Java transformation

In the final phase, you use AWS Transform to automatically convert validated COBOL code into Java Spring Boot applications. Generate production-ready Java code with the intelligent refactoring in AWS Transform. This refactoring preserves the business logic validated in previous phases while introducing modern design patterns, including dependency injection, repository patterns, and service layers.

You can deploy the resulting Java applications on AWS infrastructure to achieve cloud scalability and resilience while maintaining the same business functionality as your legacy mainframe systems. This cloud-focused approach replaces monolithic mainframe architecture with modular, maintainable code that can be independently deployed, monitored, and enhanced.

For detailed step-by-step instructions, refer to the AWS Transform Refactor Workshop.

Lessons learned

When you apply this methodology in practice, here are the key lessons that can shape your approach:

  • Human-in-the-loop validation is essential for transformation quality. Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE can help improve business rule identification, but AI-generated documents should always be treated as drafts. SME review is essential at every critical stage, not only during extraction, to catch domain-specific logic, edge cases, and business context that AI tools may overlook. This human oversight can help reduce post-deployment defects compared to automated conversion without structured checkpoints.
  • The intermediate COBOL step reduces risk. You will find the multi-stage approach (Assembler to COBOL to Java) with validation checkpoints at each phase more reliable than attempting direct conversion. The intermediate step helps you verify business logic preservation before committing to the final Java transformation.
  • A spec-driven methodology helps you prevent rework. Creating detailed functional specifications before code conversion catches misunderstandings early. With structured JSON specifications, you can also automate validation and direct integration with transformation tools.
  • Incremental validation helps you accelerate your overall timeline. Testing after each transformation stage, rather than waiting until the end, helps you detect issues early and reduces overall rework. Quality gates at each phase help confirm the output is ready for the next stage.

Conclusion and next steps

In this post, we walked through a systematic, AI-powered approach to transform legacy mainframe Assembler applications into Java applications built for the cloud on AWS. This approach combines Amazon Bedrock and Kiro IDE for intelligent business logic extraction with AWS Transform for automated COBOL-to-Java conversion. By following a multi-stage methodology with validation checkpoints at each phase, you can help accelerate modernization timelines while preserving critical business logic integrity.

To evaluate the full service landscape and understand how the components fit together, start with the AWS Mainframe Modernization documentation. When you’re ready to see the pipeline in action, the AWS Transform Refactor Workshop walks you through the end-to-end process with sample workloads you can run in your own environment. If you’d like to discuss how this approach applies to your specific environment, contact an AWS representative.

Tell us about your modernization journey and share your thoughts in the comments.

entries.title: Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
entries.summary: Novo Nordisk's Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area team built a process-intelligence assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using a GraphRAG architecture that pairs a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune with hybrid search in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless to turn millions of controlled manufacturing documents into grounded, cited answers.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization.

Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility.

Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how quickly life-saving medicines reach patients.

To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes.

We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible.

The challenge

Teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once:

  • The right document out of a large corpus.
  • The right version and lifecycle state (approved and effective, not draft or obsolete).
  • The right scope (it actually applies to the site, product generation, and equipment).
  • The relationships (which documents reference which, and what a change would impact).

Conventional keyword search returns documents, not answers, with no concept of scope, version, or relationship. A plain vector-based Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system improves recall on natural-language questions but still struggles with exact identifiers (document numbers, equipment codes), with multi-hop relationship questions, and (most importantly for a regulated domain) with identifying when relevant content is not available. The team needed a system that treats structure and relationships as first-class, stays grounded in approved sources, and clarifies instead of guessing.

Solution overview

The assistant is built on a GraphRAG architecture: a knowledge graph in Amazon Neptune captures structure and relationships, and a hybrid search index in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless provides semantic and exact-match recall over document contents. The two stores are deliberately kept separate and bridged at query time rather than combined into a single engine. This is a common production GraphRAG pattern.

The reasoning layer runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore was chosen for its managed agent runtime with built-in session isolation, native tool orchestration, and integrated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and observability. This removes undifferentiated infrastructure work so the team could focus on the domain logic. The agent runtimes are built with the Strands Agents SDK and powered by Anthropic Claude models on Amazon Bedrock. Documents are processed through an ingestion pipeline that uses Amazon Bedrock Data Automation for multimodal parsing, orchestrated with AWS Step Functions and AWS Lambda. The stack is defined as infrastructure as code with the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK).

At a high level, a question flows through the system like this:

  • The query agent receives the question and, in guided mode, determines whether the scope is clear enough to answer well.
  • If it is ambiguous, the agent asks a short, graph-grounded clarifying question (for example, which site or product generation applies) before searching.
  • After scope is clear, hybrid search retrieves candidate passages, the graph expands from those results to add structure and relationships, and a reranking step sharpens precision.
  • The agent composes an answer grounded in and cited to approved source documents, and is explicit when content is not available.

Architecture

A two-layer taxonomy: Structure plus domain detail

The graph is organized around two complementary layers, which is what lets the assistant take into account where a document sits and what it is about.

High-level taxonomy: The process tree. The organization’s official process framework is modeled as a hierarchy of process nodes (roughly three levels, parent to child). Each controlled document is attached to the lowest applicable process level, so each onboarded document has a known place. This lets the assistant scope a question to a process area before retrieving anything, and automatically categorize newly ingested documents.

Low-level taxonomy: Domain entities. SMEs define the entities that make an answer correct or incorrect in manufacturing: sites, product generations, equipment, process steps, and similar attributes. These are modeled as first-class graph nodes linked to the documents that describe them, using a small set of unified relationship types rather than an ever-growing list of edge names.

Modeling both layers is what distinguishes a genuine GraphRAG system from two databases side by side. The document number on an OpenSearch passage is also a node in the graph, so a search hit is an immediate entry point into the graph’s structure with no fuzzy re-matching required. This chunk-to-graph bridge is a key design choice in the retrieval path.

Why a fixed, curated taxonomy (and why this is best practice)

Early GraphRAG work favored open-ended extraction, letting a language model discover entities with no fixed schema. This approach is powerful for open-ended sensemaking over sprawling text, but it is noisy, hard to maintain, and difficult to audit. Over the past couple of years, the consensus has shifted toward ontology-guided extraction using a predefined, domain-specific schema to guide the model, which improves accuracy and reliability for specialized corpora.

For regulated pharmaceutical manufacturing this is not a compromise, but the right default. The domain already has a real ontology, curated by experts, and a fixed schema with a human-in-the-loop promotion process for new entities supports the auditability the team needed in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The design aligns with where much of the field has moved since early open-schema approaches, while making design decisions easier to explain to quality and audit stakeholders.

Retrieval: Hybrid search, graph expansion, and reranking

Each store covers the other’s blind spot:

  • OpenSearch provides recall – Hybrid search combines dense vector similarity (Amazon Titan Text Embeddings) with lexical BM25 matching, fused with reciprocal rank fusion. Vector search captures meaning. And lexical matching catches the exact tokens that matter here: document numbers, equipment codes, and multilingual terminology.
  • Neptune provides structure – Given the entities and documents search surfaced, the graph answers “what is connected, how, and how far”: neighboring documents, references, position in the hierarchy, and impact of a change, which is exactly what vector-only retrieval cannot do.

A common pattern is vector finds the seeds, the graph expands from them, and the reverse for relationship-first questions. A reranking stage (a cross-encoder through Amazon Bedrock Rerank) sits after fusion: it reads the question and each candidate passage together and reorders them, adding a precision pass on top of the cheaper recall stage before anything reaches the model.

Guided mode: Clarify before you retrieve

A distinctive part of the assistant is how it handles ambiguity. A question like “which samples are taken on the granulator?” has several correct answers depending on product generation, site, equipment, and batch size. Answering immediately risks a confident, wrong, out-of-scope response, which is the worst outcome in a regulated setting.

Guided mode inverts the usual RAG order: instead of retrieving first, the agent narrows scope through clarification first, then searches. This follows recent research on clarifying ambiguous questions before retrieval and on using a knowledge graph to supply the clarification options rather than letting the model invent them. It uses two classes of scope:

  • A small, near-universal set of attributes (such as site and product generation) is asked directly and consistently for process-specific questions.
  • Everything deeper: which equipment, which batch size, and attributes added over time. This is all derived from the graph at query time. A scope-resolution step matches the user’s term against real graph nodes, filters by what is already known, and, if more than one candidate remains, offers the attribute that genuinely distinguishes them, using only values that exist in the graph.

This keeps clarification options grounded in real data (designed to help reduce the risk of hallucinated options) and it scales: when experts add a new distinguishing attribute to the taxonomy, the assistant surfaces it automatically, without requiring changes to prompts or code.

Grounding and trust in a regulated environment

Accuracy here is defined narrowly and enforced deliberately:

  • Explicit indexed state – A document can exist in the graph with metadata, relationships, and place in the hierarchy before its contents are searchable. A deterministic flag tracks whether a document’s content is indexed, so the assistant can distinguish between “I have this document’s contents” and “I only have its metadata,” rather than inferring availability from empty search results.
  • Approved sources by default – Answers rely on approved and effective documents and the latest applicable version, unless the user explicitly asks for drafts or historical revisions.
  • Anti-hallucination rules – Clarification options and cited claims are designed to come from actual tool results rather than the model’s own knowledge.
  • Stated limitations – When retrieved material is missing or ambiguous, the assistant says so rather than filling the gap and flags when SME, quality, or regulatory review is needed.

An automated evaluation harness checks responses against these criteria: relevant-source selection, valid document status, latest applicable version, scope compliance, citation accuracy, and faithful preservation of requirement strength (must, should, or may) so behavior can be measured as the system evolves.

An intelligent search engine over a vault of millions of documents

The wider vault this solution sits on top of holds on the order of four million documents. At that scale, the problem is not a shortage of information but the near-impossibility of finding the exactly right, in-scope, current answer by hand. Traditional enterprise search returns long lists ranked by keyword overlap and leaves the hard work to the person asking. This includes deciding which result applies, which version is effective, and how documents relate.

This solution turns the vault into an intelligent, answer-first search engine, and the two-layer taxonomy is what makes that tractable at scale:

  • The graph is the full map and the index is the searchable subset. Each onboarded document across all registered domains is placed in the graph with its metadata, relationships, and hierarchy position. This means the assistant can reason about where a document sits and how it connects, even for the millions whose contents are not yet indexed. Full-text contents are indexed for onboarded domains, added incrementally, and the assistant is explicit about which is which.
  • Scope narrows the search space before retrieval. Because guided mode resolves site, product generation, process area, and equipment up front, a question is filtered to the small slice of the vault that can answer it. The system searches the few documents in scope, not millions. This helps keep answers precise as the corpus grows.
  • Hybrid search plus graph expansion goes beyond keyword ranking, surfacing related documents, references, and hierarchy a ranked list would never reveal, and returning a grounded, cited answer (not ten blue links) while saying when content is unavailable.

The design is intended to scale with the vault rather than degrade as it grows: the larger and more interconnected the documentation, the more value the graph and scoping add.

Outcomes

Depending on the type of task an SME is doing (searching for an answer, updating a document, or adapting one for a new context), work that used to take hours or days is reduced to minutes. Beyond raw time saved, the solution changes what is practical to do at all:

  • Navigate the group’s process landscape – Users can move across all three levels of the process taxonomy, spanning roughly four million documents and their many subprocesses through a single assistant that acts as both a search engine and a guide over the documentation, the process, and the organizational maps.
  • Consolidate structured and unstructured data – Metadata, process hierarchy, and document contents are unified into one searchable knowledge graph, so information that used to live in separate systems can be queried together.
  • Understand relationships between entities and documents – The graph helps users ask how documents, processes, equipment, sites, and products connect, including multi-hop questions that manual search cannot answer.
  • Trace and validate references end to end – The solution can map a document’s full chain of references and flag where a document points at out-of-date or superseded material, surfacing integrity issues across the corpus rather than one document at a time.
  • Extend to further AI and agentic capabilities – The same grounded foundation opens the door to capabilities like document generation, revision with impact analysis, and other agentic workflows reusing the same graph, retrieval, and guardrails rather than starting from scratch.

Just as important in a regulated setting, the assistant’s design to clarify scope and flag missing or ambiguous content helps reduce the risk of confident, out-of-scope answers, where the real cost of a mistake lies.

A collaborative delivery model

The Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area collaborated with AWS to build this solution, with subject-matter experts and data and AI engineers working closely throughout. The taxonomy that makes the assistant accurate comes directly from the group’s domain experts. The retrieval and agent architecture was designed and iterated with AWS.

Building a prototype was key to getting the solution to go live. Rather than debating capabilities in the abstract, the team put a working system in front of subject-matter experts early. They tested it against real questions and used what they learned to sharpen the taxonomy, the retrieval path, and the guided-mode behavior. The prototype turned an ambitious idea into something people could try, critique, and trust. It also de-risked the architecture decisions before any broader rollout.

Conclusion

By combining a curated knowledge graph, hybrid search, and a clarify-before-retrieve agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the Novo Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area built a process-intelligence assistant that is fast where speed helps and grounded where accuracy matters. The design applies current GraphRAG patterns to regulated manufacturing: ontology-guided extraction, a bridged two-store retrieval path, graph-grounded disambiguation, and reranking. This turns a large documentation landscape into grounded, cited answers with room to extend to new domains.

To get started building your own agentic AI solution, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for managed agent runtime, tool orchestration, and observability at scale. The agent runtimes in this post were built with the Strands Agents SDK, an open source, framework agnostic toolkit you can use with your own retrieval stack. For GraphRAG reference architectures using Amazon Neptune and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, visit the AWS Architecture Center.

entries.title: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
entries.summary: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so agentic retrieval can answer questions over CSV, XLSX, and XLS files. It looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row, then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer multi-step analytical questions.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps.

A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook.

Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same 

AgenticRetrieveStream
request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read.

In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read.

Why tables are hard for retrieval

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape:

  • Long tables – A table with thousands of rows spans many passages, and retrieval returns only the few that best match the question. An answer built from them uses a handful of rows, so a total, a comparison, or a threshold check can be incomplete.
  • Wide tables – In a table with hundreds of columns, one row can hold more text than a passage or a search model takes in at once. As a result, values in later columns are harder to match. Long passages from wide tables can also match many unrelated questions and push more relevant passages out of the results.

Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy.

Tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps.

Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?”

ComparedRetrieve onlyAgentic retrieval with tabular search
What you get backPassages from the policy, memo, business review, and workbook, but no complete answerAn answer naming Sales, Engineering, and Operations, with each department’s variance against its revised budget
Revised variance percentagesNot available. No file stores them, so no passage can contain themCalculated from every department row in the final workbook
SourcesEach passage links to its own file, but none of them contains the answerCitations to the finance policy and the close memo. The trace names the workbook the code read

Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search.

How tabular search works in agentic retrieval

In agentic retrieval, an agent uses retrieval to decide which documents matter and then writes the answer. Tabular search is part of that flow, so there’s nothing to turn on.

When a question needs the data in a table, the request moves through these stages:

  • Retrieve – Passages come back, including passages from a table file.
  • Plan – The agent uses the question and table structure to determine whether to run code over one or more retrieved tables.
  • Stage – Tabular search copies the original file into an isolated sandbox with no network access.
  • Compute – Model-written code runs over the whole table or sheet.
  • Return – The agent gets back only what the code prints, such as totals or matching rows.
  • Answer – The agent answers from the results and the passages, with citations.

Tabular search starts when retrieved passages come from a CSV, XLSX, or XLS file and the question needs a calculation across rows or a lookup of specific values.

Knowledge bases, connectors, and APIs

An 

AgenticRetrieveStream
request can search one knowledge base or several. The 
Retrieve
API keeps returning passages and doesn’t run code.

Tabular search works the same way whichever connector brings the files into the knowledge base, including Amazon S3, Microsoft SharePoint, Atlassian Confluence, and others.

Scope and trade-offs

Tabular search is built for questions that need calculations or lookups over the table files it retrieves. Running code adds at least one more agent turn, so answers that use table data take longer than text-only answers. Governed metrics, recurring dashboards, warehouse-scale joins, and reporting controls still belong in your business intelligence (BI) tools. Tabular search works on table files stored next to your documents, and you don’t define a schema.

Solution overview

In this solution, an Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base stores your CSV and Excel files together with related documents, such as PDF and Word files. Your application sends every question through agentic retrieval. When a question needs table data, the answer combines calculations over your tables with facts from your documents. It cites the passages it used, and the trace names the table files the code read.

In Figure 1, an Amazon S3 data source syncs these files into the knowledge base, which keeps embeddings, text, metadata, and the original files. When your application sends a question with 

AgenticRetrieveStream
, agentic retrieval plans the work and retrieves passages from the knowledge base. If the question needs data from a table file, it sends the files to read to an isolated sandbox with no network access. There, model-written code runs over the original file and returns printed results. The answer, with citations and trace events, streams back to your application.

The worked example uses fictitious AnyCompany Retail finance files:

  • Final P&L workbook (
    anycompany-pnl-fy2026.xlsx
    ). It has Notes, Actuals, Budget, and Summary sheets, with one row per month, cost center, and account in the Actuals and Budget sheets.
  • Draft workbook. A preliminary copy with different Q3 numbers.
  • Finance variance policy (PDF). Defines controllable spend and approved budget, and sets review thresholds.
  • Q3 close memo (Word). Lists approved and rejected budget revisions.
  • Business review (Markdown). Explains the main variances.

These files are in the tabular-search folder of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns GitHub repository. The folder also has an AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app that deploys the resources in this post, and Python scripts that ask these questions.

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • Permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, S3 buckets, and Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases.
  • For the identity that calls 
    AgenticRetrieveStream
    , the permissions for agentic retrieval, including 
    bedrock:GetDocumentContent
    . The agent reads the original table file with the caller’s credentials.
  • Amazon Bedrock in an AWS Region where tabular search is available. For Region availability, see Supported AWS Regions.
  • Your own CSV, XLSX, or XLS files and related documents.
  • To follow the walkthrough: Python 3.10 or later with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) version 1.43.123 or later. You can also ask questions from the knowledge base test window in the Amazon Bedrock console or with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI).

The calling identity needs this policy, from the agentic retrieval documentation:

For costs, see Amazon Bedrock pricing.

Upload your files to Amazon S3

Put the table files and related documents under one prefix.

  • Open the Amazon S3 console and choose Create bucket.
  • Enter a globally unique bucket name (this post uses 
    amzn-s3-demo-bucket
    ), keep Block all public access selected, and choose Create bucket.
  • Choose the bucket, choose Create folder, and enter 
    finance
    .
  • Open the 
    finance
    folder and choose Upload.
  • Choose Add files, select your table files and documents, and choose Upload.

Create the knowledge base and data source

The knowledge base needs an IAM role that Amazon Bedrock can assume. This trust policy allows only the 

bedrock.amazonaws.com
service principal, and only for knowledge bases in your account.

Next, set up the remaining resources:

  • Create a role named 
    kb-finance-role
    with the trust policy.
  • Attach an inline policy that allows 
    s3:ListBucket
    on the bucket and 
    s3:GetObject
    on its objects.
  • Create a knowledge base of type 
    MANAGED
    with the managed embedding model.
  • Create a 
    MANAGED_KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTOR
    data source for the bucket, limited to the 
    finance/
    prefix.
  • Set 
    maxFileSizeInMegaBytes
    above your largest file.

The inline policy for step 2 allows reads on this bucket only:

This script runs steps 3 to 5 and prints the IDs:

Sync the data source and check file types

Tabular search can start only if the knowledge base assigns the right file type, so check the file type after the first sync.

  • Start an ingestion job for the data source.
  • Poll the job until its status is 
    COMPLETE
    .
  • Review the job statistics for failed documents.
  • Run a 
    Retrieve
    call with your question.
  • Confirm that table passages show 
    _file_type
    as 
    CSV
    (for CSV files) or 
    MS_EXCEL
    (for XLSX and XLS files).

The first script runs steps 1 to 3:

The second script runs steps 4 and 5 so you can check the table file type before asking the question with agentic retrieval. With your own files, ask a question that pairs a rule in one of your documents with a calculation over your tables, and name both.

Ask a question across tables and documents

Send the same question through 

AgenticRetrieveStream
. The script prints the answer, each 
CodeExecution
status, and the files the code read.

For these files, the answer combines two workbook tables with two documents:

  • From the documents. The finance policy defines controllable spend as the Contractors, Travel, Software, and Marketing Programs accounts, which leaves out salaries and facilities. The business review explains the main variances.
  • From the tables. The code uses every row in the Actuals and Budget sheets, filters both to fiscal Q2 and the four accounts, and then compares cost centers.
  • Answer. CC-3010 (Platform) is over by 124,559.90 US dollars, with actual spending of 394,859.90 against a budget of 270,300.00. The business review attributes the variance to contractors brought in for a data platform migration. Counting every operating expense account instead gives 133,434.05.

Read the trace

Trace events arrive in this order:

  • Planning. A 
    Planning
    event with status 
    SUCCEEDED
    includes a 
    codeExecution
    action that names the documents the code will read.
  • The code step. A 
    CodeExecution
    event with status 
    IN_PROGRESS
    (“Running code over 1 document(s)”), then one with status 
    SUCCEEDED
    . The 
    SUCCEEDED
    message names each file the code read and its size.
  • The answer. A second planning round and the response text precede a final 
    result
    event that includes the citations. Citations point to the passages the answer used, so a table file the code read isn’t always among them.

In this example, the 

Planning
event names only the final workbook, because the policy and the business review arrive as retrieved passages.

On longer calls, the stream repeats the 

IN_PROGRESS
event every 10 seconds, so a read timeout doesn’t fire. A code step that can’t finish reports 
FAILED
, and the agent usually retries or falls back.

Tabular search runs as part of response generation, which is on by default, so the script leaves 

generateResponse
unset. If you set 
generateResponse
to false, the agent returns retrieval results without running code. For details, see agentic retrieval.

Try more questions

Each of the following questions also pairs a document with the workbook.

Apply memo revisions to quarterly totals

This question needs a budget that exists only after the memo’s revisions:

The answer uses the revisions from the memo and the Q3 actuals and original budget from the workbook. Spending came in 49,572.40 US dollars under the revised budget, so the answer is yes, even though the same spending is over the original budget. Plain 

Retrieve
returns memo and workbook passages, but none of them contains these figures.

Apply a policy threshold after budget revisions

Here is the full version of the finance team’s question from the introduction. It needs the policy’s threshold, the memo’s revisions, and the workbook:

The policy requires commentary when the variance exceeds 5 percent of the approved budget, which includes approved revisions, and the memo approves a Marketing increase and an Engineering cut. The answer is Sales (-6.50 percent), Engineering (+5.79 percent), and Operations (+6.20 percent). Engineering crosses the threshold only because the approved cut lowers its budget.

Continue the conversation

Tabular search also works in multi-turn conversations. Send earlier turns in 

messages
, and it runs in whichever turn needs the table. This first question asks for a calculation from the workbook:

For the follow-up, send the first question, its answer (

"role": "assistant"
), and the new question in 
messages
:

The variance is 12.40 percent over budget, so it needs written commentary. Because it exceeds 10 percent, the policy also requires review by the CFO, Nikki Wolf. Here, the first turn usually runs code over the workbook, and the second answers the policy question from the history.

For longer sessions, you can keep conversation history in an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore memory resource by setting 

memoryConfiguration
on the request, instead of resending earlier turns. For details, see agentic retrieval.

Best practices for questions over tables

Word your questions with care, because retrieval picks which table the code reads. Focused questions that name their sources help retrieval pick the right table.

  • Pair one rule with one table. Name the document that holds the rule, such as “as revised in the Q3 close memo.”
  • Name the file when there is more than one version. For example, “use the final FY2026 P&L workbook, anycompany-pnl-fy2026.xlsx.”
  • Ask for the calculation when you want one. If a summary sheet holds a figure, the agent can answer from it. Say “Calculate each department’s variance from the Actuals and Budget sheets” to compute from detail rows.
  • Ask focused questions. Build larger analyses over several turns.

A few data and application choices help as well:

  • Keep tables in CSV, XLSX, or XLS files. Export tables from PDF or Word documents first.
  • Set the file size filter above your largest table. Files larger than 
    maxFileSizeInMegaBytes
    aren’t ingested, so the code can’t read them.
  • Keep Excel sheets within 200 MB. As of this writing, tabular search runs code over CSV files up to 500 MB, the ingestion limit, but over Excel sheets only up to 200 MB. You can still ingest larger Excel files, so check sheet sizes before you rely on full-table calculations.
  • Use tabular search for analysis. Running code adds an agent turn, so keep plain 
    Retrieve
    for quick lookups in text.
  • Scope files with metadata filters. A filter under 
    retrievalOverrides
    , for example on 
    _document_title
    , controls which files the code can read.
  • Audit with the trace. The generated code isn’t returned, by design, because it can echo cell values. The trace shows which files the code read.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete these resources in order:

  • In the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Knowledge Bases, then choose 
    finance-kb
    .
  • Select the 
    finance-s3
    data source and choose Delete.
  • Delete the 
    finance-kb
    knowledge base.
  • In the Amazon S3 console, select the bucket, choose Empty, and then choose Delete, unless other workloads use it.
  • In the IAM console, choose Roles, select 
    kb-finance-role
    , and choose Delete.

If you deployed with the AWS CDK app from the repository, run 

npx cdk destroy
from its 
infra
folder instead of these steps. It deletes everything the stack created.

Conclusion

The finance team members need to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” With tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can answer that question with one agentic retrieval request that uses the workbook, the policy, and the memo together.

In this post, you learned how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also built a knowledge base with sample finance files and used the trace to see which file the code read.

To get started, see Build a managed knowledge base and agentic retrieval in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, and AgenticRetrieveStream in the Amazon Bedrock API Reference. To learn more, read Build enterprise search for agents with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base on the AWS Artificial Intelligence Blog.

entries.title: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
entries.summary: With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail matches by meaning rather than keyword, which can block more than you intend. This post presents eight best practices for writing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don't.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails

With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended.

When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns:

  • Topics that block legitimate queries. A topic framed around a subject domain (Finance, Legal, Compensation) rather than the user’s intention can match queries semantically near that domain. This is a frequent failure mode.
  • Topics that miss the requests they were written to catch. A definition built from keyword lists (“words like invest, portfolio, stock…”) misses phrasings that use other vocabulary and fires on unrelated inputs that happen to share those words.
  • Examples that teach the wrong thing. Five paraphrases of one idea leave the topic’s boundaries unguarded, and examples that name specific countries, products, or companies pull those entities into the topic’s context.
  • Topics that interfere with each other. Overlapping definitions compete for the same input, report matches inconsistently, and can together block inputs that neither would block alone.

The rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t.

The scenario: AnyCompany Bank’s customer assistant

To ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things.

Application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope.

Must-block list (from legal and compliance):

  • Personalized investment recommendations (a regulatory line, because AnyCompany Bank isn’t registered as an investment adviser through this channel).
  • Legal counsel or litigation guidance regarding disputes against AnyCompany Bank.
  • Insider-trading advice (a specific slice of financial advice with its own regulatory weight).
  • Descriptions of how to build weapons (universal safety, not domain-specific).
  • Prompt injection or jailbreak attempts (a different kind of signal, because the request is trying to override the assistant’s own instructions).
  • Repeating specific named competitor products in AnyCompany Bank’s outputs.

Must-pass list (the things the assistant exists to do):

  • Account balance and statement questions.
  • Transfer instructions, payoff quotes, escrow questions.
  • Card management, fraud reports (routed to a human), lost-card replacement.
  • Mortgage servicing operations, such as modifications, forbearance, and payment plans.
  • General financial-literacy questions (“What is a certificate of deposit?”), phrased as education rather than personalized advice.

Against that target, AnyCompany Bank’s team first drafted four topics, all of them currently blocking legitimate queries:

Every one of these topics names a subject domain the assistant works in, rather than the intention the bank needs to refuse. Fixing this is what the rest of the post is about. The next eight sections work through the practices, most of them closing with a “Back at AnyCompany Bank” subsection that shows the fix applied to this scenario. The post then closes with the one limitation to plan for regardless of how well you follow the practices: results are not fully deterministic.

Note: Denied Topic structure in Standard tier. A topic has three parts, a name, a definition, and up to five examples, and the guardrail evaluates all three together as a single unit, not the definition alone. The name can be up to 100 characters. The definition can be up to 1,000 characters, with 100–300 as the practical sweet spot. Each example can be up to 100 characters, and a guardrail can hold up to 30 topics.

Best practice 1: Frame the topic around the user’s intention, not the subject domain

This practice sets the general frame. Best practices 2 through 4 apply it to each part of a topic in turn: the name, the definition, and the examples.

A frequent reason a topic blocks legitimate queries is that the topic describes a subject domain rather than what the user wants from the exchange. Two queries in the same domain can carry different intentions. “When does my direct deposit clear?” and “How much does an L5 engineer earn?” both concern pay, but only the second is a salary comparison. A domain-framed topic collapses those distinctions and can block queries semantically near the domain. A topic framed around the user’s intention matches only queries where that intention is present.

Intention is the framing lens. To make it operational, name the topic after the specific action or content type that expresses the intention on the surface, such as a request, a claim, or a piece of generated content. Intention tells you what to catch, and action gives you a concrete shape the guardrail can evaluate.

The guardrail evaluates both the topic name and its definition together. When either component names a domain, the topic matches too broadly. When both name an action that expresses a specific intention, the topic is precise.

Guidelines

  • Identify the intention. State briefly, in your own words, what the user is trying to get from the assistant that you want to refuse, such as a personalized recommendation, a legal opinion, private contact details, or a partisan endorsement. This is the diagnostic step, and it doesn’t appear verbatim in the topic.
  • Name the topic after the action that expresses that intention. Use a phrase that describes a specific action or behavior, not a broad subject area. The phrase can be an action-derived noun (Investment Recommendations, Salary Comparisons), a specific behavior noun phrase (Colleague Arguments, Passport and Visa Renewal), or a verb-ing form (Suing for Damages). See Best practice 2 for details.
  • If your topic name is a category noun (Banking, Compensation, Security, Legal, Finance), the topic is domain-framed. Rename it after the action that expresses the intention you actually want to block.
  • Rewrite your definition to begin with the action. Openers such as “Asking for X”, “Requests for Y”, “Statements that describe Z”, or “Generating W” express the intention through a specific action. Avoid subject-area openers such as “Related to X”, “Content about Y”, or “Anything mentioning Z”.

The next few best practices apply this idea to AnyCompany Bank’s own topics, with concrete examples. Best practice 2 renames them, and Best practice 3 tightens their definitions to match.

Best practice 2: Choose an actionable topic name

The topic name has a meaningful effect on what is matched, often greater than expected. A broad category name (Finance, Security, Legal) can lead the guardrail to associate the topic with vocabulary in that category, even when the definition attempts to narrow the scope. A specific action name (Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, Suing for Damages) helps narrow the scope before the definition is read.

Guidelines

  • Prefer a specific action or behavior phrase (2–5 words). Avoid single-word category labels.
  • The following forms can work, as long as the phrase describes a specific action or behavior rather than a broad subject area:
    • Action-noun form: an activity-derived noun as the head, such as Investment Recommendations, Hacking Instructions, or Election Fraud Claims.
    • Specific behavior noun phrase: a noun phrase that names a specific behavior, such as Colleague Arguments, Passport and Visa Renewal, or Underage Self-Statement.
    • Verb-ing form: an -ing verb followed by an object, such as Suing for Damages or Requesting Contact Details for Named Individuals. This form is useful when the action requires a verb to be clear.
  • Read the name aloud and ask whether it describes something the user is doing or only a subject area the user’s query is near. If the name only names a subject area, rename it.
  • Avoid names that include broad institutional labels (Government, Company, Insurance) unless the action is specifically about that institution. Institutional labels can produce unintended matches. For example, a topic named Government Documents might match queries that mention a country name plus a document, even if the query is about internal company policy.

Back at AnyCompany Bank

One of AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topics was named Legal:

This is why “Can you help me modify my mortgage?” got blocked. Mortgages are legal instruments, so queries about them live in the semantic neighborhood of legal. Renaming solves half the problem before we even touch the definition:

The new name uses a verb-derived noun (litigation), names a second specific behavior (non-servicing legal advice), and makes clear by contrast that servicing questions, such as modifications, forbearance, and escrow, are outside the topic. The name itself now carries some of the work the definition would otherwise do alone.

AnyCompany Bank applied the same logic to the Fraud topic, renaming it to Fraud Investigation Requests. The assistant should still let customers report fraud, which gets routed to a human, but must not attempt to investigate fraud claims itself.

After these three renames, AnyCompany Bank’s topic list is:

Best practice 3: Write action-scoped definitions

The definition should describe the user’s action on a specific object, rather than the general subject of that action.

Guidelines

  • Begin with the action or the content type. Open the definition with a phrase that names what the user is doing or producing. Common effective openers include:
    • “Asking for…”, “Requesting…”, “Requests for…”, “Requests to…”, “Seeking…”, “Recommending…”, when the topic covers user requests for a specific action.
    • “Statements that…”, “Providing…”, “Generating…”, “Content that includes…”, when the topic covers user-produced content, disclosures, or generated output.
    • “Using X to Y”, when the topic covers a specific technique or method.
  • Avoid opening with a subject-area phrase such as “Related to X”, “Content about Y”, or “Anything mentioning Z”, which is domain-framed rather than action-framed.
  • Specify the objects. State what the user is asking about, using concrete items rather than broad categories, for example, “individual stocks, bonds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” rather than “financial products”.
  • Add discriminating detail. If two topics share vocabulary (for example, both involve “customer”), give each definition a distinct feature so the guardrail can differentiate them. Definitions that share meaning cause the two topics to interfere with each other.
  • Keep the definition positive. Describe what is in scope. Short trailing exclusions can help disambiguate. See Best practice 8 for cases where exclusions are harmful.
  • Length isn’t the goal. Longer definitions are not necessarily better, and a longer definition can increase the topic’s sensitivity to the wording of neighboring topics.

Structural template

We recommend the following structure:

[Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases].

Back at AnyCompany Bank

AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic was named Finance, with a definition to match:

This is exactly why “Where can I find my payoff quote?” was blocked. Payoff is a financial term, quote concerns money, and the input is “related to” the finance domain, even though the customer’s intention, retrieving a servicing figure, has nothing to do with what AnyCompany Bank wanted to refuse.

Following Best practice 1, the team renamed the topic to Investment Recommendations and adjusted the definition’s vocabulary to match, without yet making it action-scoped:

This was still domain-framed even though the name had improved. General education (“Explain what a mutual fund is”), historical financial news (“Why did rates rise last quarter?”), and portfolio review (“Show me my holdings”) all matched. The assistant should answer all of them.

The team applied the structural template, with an action opener, specific objects, a qualifying constraint, and one or two sub-cases:

Every piece of the template serves a specific purpose. “Asking for a personalized recommendation to…” is the action opener. “Stocks, bonds, mutual funds, ETFs, or cryptocurrencies” are the specific objects. “For the user’s own investment returns” is the qualifying constraint that excludes educational and third-party discussion. The “Includes…” clause names two sub-cases: a specific-security question and an allocation-percentage question.

AnyCompany Bank applied the same template to the Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests topics:

The team now had three named topics with action-scoped definitions.

Best practice 4: Use boundary examples, not paraphrases

Examples teach the guardrail where the boundaries of your topic are. Not every example does this equally well. Five paraphrases of the same idea teach the guardrail nothing new, while five carefully chosen examples can draw the outline of the topic with much less definition text. The examples that carry the most weight are the ones sitting near the topic’s edge, close enough to a plausible non-match that they show the guardrail where to draw the line. We call these boundary examples. A good boundary example has three properties. First, it’s inside the topic’s scope. Second, it’s close to a plausible non-match, using vocabulary or structure that resembles inputs the topic should not match. Third, it differs from your other examples in sub-case, sentence shape, and vocabulary.

Guidelines

  • Use all five examples, because five varied examples are more effective than two obvious ones.
  • Cover different sub-cases. If the topic covers “buy” and “sell” advice, include examples of both.
  • Cover different sentence shapes. Include direct questions (What should I buy?), imperatives (Recommend a stock), and narrative statements (I’m considering putting money into…).
  • Include one example that is near the boundary of the topic but still inside, a borderline version of a match.
  • Don’t include country names, product names, competitor names, or company names in examples unless the topic is inherently about that specific entity. Named entities in examples create associations that cause the topic to match unrelated queries mentioning the same entity.

Back at AnyCompany Bank

The team’s first pass at examples for Investment Recommendations looked like this:

These are five ways of asking the same question. During testing, the assistant blocked “Should I buy stocks?” reliably. But it let through “Is it a good time to rotate my portfolio out of equities into bonds?”, which is exactly the kind of question the topic is supposed to catch. The paraphrases had crowded around one point in the topic, and other points were unguarded.

The rewrite spread the examples across sub-cases and sentence shapes:

These are five different sub-cases (specific stock, asset-class shift, allocation, sell timing, growth screen) and five different sentence shapes, all inside the topic. Adjacent non-matches like “Explain what an ETF is” (educational) and “Show me my portfolio report” (data retrieval) are sufficiently different from the examples that the guardrail should not match them.

The team applied the same treatment to Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice and Fraud Investigation Requests. The original Litigation examples were all variants of “Can I sue?” The rewritten set covered lawsuit filing, formal legal opinions, class-action inquiries, damages, and rights-interpretation. The original Fraud Investigation Requests examples were all variants of “Someone stole my money, what do I do?” The rewritten set covered unauthorized-charge investigation, card-fraud tracing, transaction reversal, identity-theft adjudication, and scammer tracing. Each rewritten set covers five different sub-cases inside one topic.

At this point, AnyCompany Bank’s three topics pass every test written so far. One more problem only shows up after the assistant runs against real traffic.

Best practice 5: Anchor definitions to a specific context when needed

Some concepts are inherently ambiguous, because the same words describe both a matching and non-matching action, depending on context. In these cases, add an explicit anchor that fixes the context: an institutional setting, a stated purpose, or a dual condition of the form “only applies when both X and Y are present”.

Guidelines

  • Add a physical or institutional context in which the action occurs. For a passport topic, anchor to “at an embassy or consulate” or “through an official government application process”.
  • Add a purpose qualifier. For an investment-recommendation topic, anchor to “for the user’s own investment returns” so that the topic excludes educational or third-party discussion.
  • Use dual conditions when a single anchor is insufficient: “Only applies when the request (1) explicitly mentions creating an advertising campaign AND (2) names personal identification data as the targeting criterion.”
  • Anchors should be positive (“at X”, “for Y”) rather than “except…” or “but not…”. Positive anchors describe what the topic IS.
  • Know when not to add an anchor. If the topic is already inherently narrow (a topic specifically about “insider trading”, because the phrase is unambiguous by itself), an additional anchor introduces noise. Also avoid anchoring to a proper noun that appears in many unrelated queries (“in India”, “at Amazon”). Anchor to categories (embassies, consulates) instead.
  • Check whether the topic’s own name repeats the ambiguous surface phrase. A benign, educational way of asking about the same concept often reuses that exact phrase. The guardrail reads the topic name as a signal independent of the definition (see Best practice 2). A dual-condition anchor can still lose to a name built from the term it’s trying to disambiguate.

Back at AnyCompany Bank

Adding an insider-trading topic exposed the ambiguity issue. The compliance team wanted Insider Trading Advice as a distinct topic, narrower and more serious than the general Investment Recommendations catch. The first draft:

This matched the expected case: a customer asking for a trade based on private information. It also matched something the team didn’t expect: educational queries about what insider trading is, phrased as questions. “How does the SEC define insider trading?” was getting blocked, because it “asks about insider trading”.

The team added a dual anchor:

Both conditions should rule out educational queries: they fail condition 2, because they don’t describe non-public information the user personally holds. When the team tested “How does the SEC define insider trading?” against this definition, it still got blocked some of the time. The anchor was not the problem. The topic’s name was: it repeats the exact phrase the query uses. The guardrail weighs the name as a signal independent of the definition, the same effect Best practice 2 describes elsewhere. A dual-condition anchor can specify the right conditions and still lose to a name built from the term that it’s trying to disambiguate.

The team kept the anchor and renamed the topic instead:

With the rename, the educational query passed reliably, and the real examples, the ones naming a specific security and a specific piece of non-public information, still blocked.

The definition is longer than the 100–300 character target from Best practice 3, and that is deliberate. The ambiguity here justifies the extra text. The topic itself is inherently subtle, so the definition has to carry more work.

Best practice 6: Manage topic overlap and topic count

A guardrail evaluates its topics together, not one at a time. When two topics have similar meanings, they interfere with each other. It becomes difficult to predict which topic the guardrail reports as the match, and the combined effect can block legitimate inputs that neither topic alone would block. Overlap between topics is often the reason a well-written topic produces incorrect results. The problem isn’t that topic, but a neighboring topic.

Guidelines

  • Review the whole topic set for overlap before deployment. Two topics with similar definitions cause interference even if neither is broken individually. For each new topic, ask whether the definition shares vocabulary or objects with an existing topic.
  • Be aware that topic count influences interference. As the number of topics in a single guardrail grows, the chance of interference between topics also grows, especially when several topics share vocabulary or cover related areas. If you observe topics interfering with each other and the definitions themselves look correct, consider reducing overlap between topics or distributing topics across more than one guardrail.
  • Prefer semantic diversity within a guardrail. If you have several topics on related themes (for example, three finance-adjacent topics), consider whether they belong in the same guardrail or should be separated.
  • When two topics overlap, prefer to consolidate rather than split. Merging two topics whose definitions share objects and actions is safer than attempting to draw a narrow boundary between them.
  • When a new use case appears, prefer to extend an existing topic’s examples rather than add a new near-duplicate topic. Adding a new topic changes how the guardrail interprets the entire topic set, but extending a topic’s examples doesn’t.
  • Place semantically-similar topics apart in the list. When two topics with similar wording appear next to each other, the guardrail is more likely to attribute an input to whichever it saw most recently. Interleave the list, separating related topics with an unrelated one in between.

Back at AnyCompany Bank

Suppose, late in the process, AnyCompany Bank’s compliance team proposed adding a broader Financial Advice topic alongside the already-defined Investment Recommendations. The intuition was that the broader topic would catch requests the specific one missed. Both topics were drafted with their own definitions:

The overlap became visible when the team tested “Should I put more into my 401(k)?”. Depending on how the caller ordered the topics in the API request, either Topic A, Topic B, or both would report the match, and on some orderings the guardrail blocked the input.

AnyCompany Bank consolidated. Financial Advice was removed, and Investment Recommendations was left to carry the specific action. After the consolidation, the ordering-dependent variance disappeared. The same input produced the same verdict regardless of where topics sat in the API call, which is the primary win from removing the overlap.

The 401(k) query itself, however, was not fully resolved by consolidation alone. Because “Should I put more into my 401(k)?” shares its “Should I put more…” frame with a real trading recommendation, Investment Recommendations still matches it on the surface. This is a residual boundary case that consolidation can’t fix by itself. It’s exactly the kind of structurally-similar match that Best practice 8 warns a trailing exclusion can’t reliably override.

The team also reordered the remaining topics. The original order was:

Topics 1 and 2 both discuss securities and cover related financial actions, so adjacent placement invited attribution ambiguity for borderline inputs. The team interleaved them:

Litigation and Non-Servicing Legal Advice now sits between the two securities-adjacent topics.
