Borderline questions like “Should I trade my Example Corp shares based on rumor?” now attribute more consistently to Trading on Non-Public Information rather than flipping between Trading on Non-Public Information and Investment Recommendations.

Best practice 7: Use the right policy for the job

Denied Topics is the right tool when the rule you need to enforce is specific to your business and expressible as a short description of the content. Think of a regulatory line, a policy commitment, a legal risk, or a scope boundary, rather than a universal safety category or a fixed list of words. Guardrails offers several policies that share the same goal of blocking specific content, but each is designed for a different kind of signal. Using Denied Topics for a category that another policy handles natively tends to block too much or too little, complicates your configuration, and produces worse results. A carefully written topic for a category that Content Filter already covers is usually less effective than Content Filter for that category.

Note that enabling more than one policy in the same guardrail incurs additional cost, because each enabled policy is evaluated on every request. When you compose Denied Topics with Content Filter or Prompt Attack, plan for the combined cost.

When to use each policy

What you are trying to catchRight policyCommon mistake
Broad safety categories (hate, insults, violence, sexual, misconduct)Content FilterA Denied Topics topic named Hate Speech or Violence
Prompt injection, jailbreak attemptsPrompt AttackA Denied Topics topic named Jailbreak or Instruction Override
Specific words, phrases, or product names to consistently blockWord FilterA Denied Topics topic named Blocked Terms or Competitor Names
Personal identifiers (names, phone numbers, SSN, credit cards)Sensitive Information filterA Denied Topics topic named PII Detection
Custom content categories specific to your business or policyDenied Topics(this is the correct use)
Custom content categories that also require Content Filter-like coverageCompose Denied Topics with Content FilterAttempting to reproduce Content Filter functionality in Denied Topics alone

Back at AnyCompany Bank

Looking back at AnyCompany Bank’s must-block list (from the scenario at the start of the post), three of the six items are not really Denied Topics at all. They belong to policies that Guardrails already provides natively.

  • “Descriptions of how to build weapons” is a universal safety category, not a bank-specific policy. It moves to Content Filter → VIOLENCE at HIGH strength.
  • “Repeating specific named competitor products” is exact-string blocking, not semantic matching. It moves to Word Filter with the competitor names as literal entries. (AnyCompany Bank’s first-draft topic list did include a topic called Competitors for this purpose. That topic is deleted, because Denied Topics evaluates meaning and would match ordinary mentions of the competitor’s name while missing rephrasings.)
  • “Prompt injection or jailbreak attempts” is a different signal entirely. The user is trying to override the assistant’s own instructions, not asking about a domain. It moves to Prompt Attack.

After this cleanup, AnyCompany Bank’s guardrail configuration composes multiple policies:

Denied Topics carries only the four bank-specific rules that no other policy can express.

Best practice 8: Avoid these anti-patterns

The following patterns cause topics to block the wrong inputs even when the rest of the definition is otherwise well written. Avoid them. Most are a specific case of guidance already given in earlier best practices, so each line that follows points back to where the full reasoning lives.

  • Writing the definition as an instruction to the guardrail (“Block all content related to…”) instead of a description of the topic. See Best practice 3.
  • Framing the definition mostly by what it excludes (“All content except…”) instead of what it is. See Best practice 3.
  • Listing trigger words (“Questions containing words like…”) instead of describing the concept. See Best practice 1 and Best practice 3.
  • Using Denied Topics to block a specific word, phrase, or entity type, such as a competitor name or a person’s name. Use Word Filter or the Sensitive Information filter instead. See Best practice 7.
  • Naming countries, products, competitors, or companies in examples, unless the topic is inherently about that entity. See Best practice 4.
  • Writing examples that paraphrase the definition instead of marking its boundary. See Best practice 4.
  • Writing a vague definition and relying on the examples to carry the meaning. See Best practice 3 and Best practice 4.

Trailing exclusions: A caveat and a general guide

A short trailing exclusion isn’t a general-purpose fix for every false refusal. It reliably rules out queries that are categorically different from the topic, such as a different intent, a different asker, or a different type of content. It’s less reliable when a benign query is worded almost exactly like the definition’s positive language, only about a different object. In that case, the exclusion competes against wording it closely resembles, and the match often wins.

For that structurally-similar case, prefer one of these three alternatives instead:

  • A dual-condition anchor that names the confusable case directly as part of the definition (see Best practice 5).
  • A rename that promotes the discriminator into the topic name itself, so the gate is visible before the definition is read (see Best practice 2).
  • An upstream intent-routing step that hands the ambiguous case to a specialized flow before Guardrails sees it.

A trailing exclusion remains the right first move for every other case. Reach for one of these three only when testing shows the exclusion is losing to a near-identical match.

Limitation: Results are not fully deterministic

Even a guardrail that follows every practice in this post won’t produce fully deterministic results across every possible input. Denied Topics reads meaning with a language model, and language-model evaluations carry some inherent variance. There are two forms of this variance you should plan for.

Variance when repeating the exact same request. Sending the identical input to the identical guardrail configuration two times in a row can, in rare cases, produce different results. The same characters go in, the same topic list applies, everything is the same, and yet one call blocks and the next passes. For most inputs, and for topics that follow the preceding guidance, this doesn’t happen, and the result is stable across repeated calls. The exceptions are borderline inputs, whose meaning sits close to the semantic edge of a topic. Those are the ones prone to flipping on repeat. The more precisely a topic is defined (action-scoped, specific objects, clear anchor, boundary examples), the fewer of your inputs fall in that borderline zone.

Variance when the topic list changes. The guardrail evaluates all topics together with the input on every request. Changes to the topic list, such as adding a topic, removing one, or reordering the same topics, can shift results for previously-tested inputs. An input that was blocked with one topic list might pass with a different one. This effect happens more when two topics share meaning or when a topic definition is broad. It happens less when every topic in the list has a specific, action-scoped definition and clear boundary examples. Applying the practices in this post meaningfully reduces both forms of variance.

How to plan for it

  • Don’t treat a single evaluation as proof of correctness. For an input that matters, test it multiple times, and test it as part of a small representative evaluation set rather than in isolation.
  • Keep an evaluation set that includes borderline cases. These are the inputs most likely to shift when you change something. Include a mix of clear-match, clear-non-match, and near-boundary cases.
  • Retest after changes to the topic set. Adding a topic, renaming one, tuning a definition, or reordering the list can shift results on inputs that previously behaved as expected.
  • For inputs where correctness is critical, don’t rely on Denied Topics alone. Compose it with other policies (Content Filter, Prompt Attack, Sensitive Information filter) so that no single policy is the sole line of defense on a high-stakes decision.
  • Design your product so that a wrong block is recoverable. Route blocked inputs to a human when the topic is high-stakes, give the user a way to rephrase, and log blocks with reason codes so you can audit and improve the topic set over time.

Note: Every pass-or-fail claim in this post was tested end-to-end against Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (Standard tier), each query repeated multiple times to confirm the result was stable.

Key takeaways

To recap, the practices in this post come down to eight points:

  • Frame every topic around the user’s intention, expressed as a specific action. Diagnose what the user is trying to get, then name the topic after the action that expresses that intention, not the subject area the query is near. Use “Investment Recommendations”, not “Finance”.
  • Write the definition to describe what the topic is. Use an action or content-type opener, name the concrete objects, add a qualifying constraint, and include one or two sub-cases.
  • Use up to five boundary examples. Cover different sub-cases and sentence shapes. Don’t paraphrase the definition, and avoid country, product, and competitor names.
  • Anchor ambiguous topics with a context or purpose. Use institutional settings (“at an embassy”) or purpose qualifiers (“for the user’s own investment returns”). Use dual conditions when a single anchor isn’t enough.
  • Manage overlap and topic count. Consolidate topics that share vocabulary, keep semantically-similar topics apart in the list, and retest after changes.
  • Use the right policy for the job. Denied Topics is for custom, business-specific topics. Content Filter, Word Filter, Sensitive Information, and Prompt Attack cover the categories they were designed for.
  • Avoid the seven anti-patterns. Instructions in place of descriptions, negative-only framing, keyword lists, entity capture, named entities in examples, paraphrase-only examples, and placeholder definitions all produce topics that block the wrong inputs.
  • Plan for the fact that results are not fully deterministic. Keep a borderline evaluation set, retest after every change, and design the product so a wrong block is recoverable.

Conclusion

Denied Topics is a powerful policy. With it, you can describe a bespoke content category in a short natural-language definition, without training a classifier or hand-crafting regular expressions. That power depends on describing the category the way the guardrail reads it: as the user’s intention, expressed as a specific action on a specific object, not as a subject domain. Get the framing right and the rest of the practices in this post, such as naming, definition, examples, anchors, overlap management, and policy selection, fall into place naturally.

To apply this in your own application:

  • Audit your existing topics. For each topic, ask whether the name describes an action or a subject area. Rename the ones that describe a subject area.
  • Rewrite each definition against the template: 
    [Action or content-type opener] for [specific objects] by [qualifying constraint or purpose]. Includes [one or two sub-cases].
  • Move every non-topic signal to the right policy. Send universal safety to Content Filter, specific strings to Word Filter, identifiers to the Sensitive Information filter, and jailbreak attempts to Prompt Attack.
  • Build a small evaluation set that includes both obvious matches and near-boundary non-matches drawn from your real traffic. Retest after every change to the guardrail.

To get started, visit the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails console and the Amazon Bedrock Guardrails documentation for the full policy reference and API details, including CreateGuardrail and ApplyGuardrail.

entries.title: Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
entries.summary: Retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy for each tenant on shared knowledge bases. This post shows how to give each tenant its own answers, keep tenant data apart with metadata filters, scope access with IAM tags, and roll out changes one tenant at a time.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Customize answers per tenant in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base

With retrieval instructions in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base, you can customize answers per tenant. The same product and policy documents often serve several audiences, such as customers in different regions or internal teams, and each audience needs its own answer. You set the voice, format, retrieval guidance, and answer policy that agentic retrieval applies to each request. Before this feature, you couldn’t set the answer style, so agentic retrieval could use a different style from one request to the next. For a fixed voice or structured output, you had to turn off response generation, call a model yourself, and maintain the prompt in every application.

Now you write that guidance once, as a managed, versioned Amazon Bedrock resource, and each request references it. When you change an instruction, you can pin a version so that each application switches to the new version when you’re ready.

Take AnyCompany Smart Home, a fictitious company that sells a home controller and room sensors in three sales regions. Its customer assistant serves all three regions, and its support, field sales, and legal teams use internal assistants that they built on the same documents. AnyCompany defines each region and internal team as a tenant here, and each needs a different answer. A customer in Sales Region Central needs Spanish with day/month/year dates, and a support agent needs a short ticket note. To keep the example compact, every tenant queries one knowledge base. However, agentic retrieval can search up to five knowledge bases in a single request, and the tenant’s instruction applies to all of them.

Retrieval instructions change how the assistant answers, but they aren’t an authorization or data-isolation boundary. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to control what each tenant can retrieve. In this post, we show how to give each tenant its own answers from shared knowledge bases while keeping each tenant’s data separate. By the end, you can roll out a change to one tenant’s instruction and confirm which version answered each request.

Why tenants need their own instructions

Tenants that share documents still differ in language, date and money conventions, voice, and which policy values they can quote. A retrieval instruction has four fields for these differences:

  • persona
    : who the assistant is, including identity, tone, and language.
  • answerFormat
    : how the answer is structured, including how it cites sources.
  • retrievalGuidance
    : how the agent interprets the question and what it prioritizes when it searches.
  • answerPolicy
    : whether and how to answer, including questions outside scope.

The 

persona
, 
answerFormat
, and 
answerPolicy
fields apply only when 
generateResponse
is 
true
, which is the default, and 
retrievalGuidance
applies either way. For details, see Create and manage retrieval instructions. Table 1 shows how the answer to the same return question changes when the request includes the Sales Region Central instruction and names the customer’s region.
ComparedNo instructionWith the instruction and the customer’s region
AnswerEvery region’s return window, then a question about where the unit was bought45 days from delivery, in Spanish
Last lineNone
Source: central-returns-addendum.md

Table 1: The same return question with and without the Sales Region Central instruction

These patterns come up across industries. An enterprise software provider can run one assistant for many of its own customers. Each customer uploads its policies, standard operating procedures, and company values, and 

persona
and 
answerPolicy
give each one its own voice and rules. A regulated enterprise can put a fixed disclaimer in 
answerPolicy
and a set citation form in 
answerFormat
, so every answer includes both. A team that sends answers to downstream code can get strict JSON from an 
answerFormat
, without a separate generation step. In each case, the documents are shared, and the voice, format, and policy change from caller to caller.

How retrieval instructions work

An instruction belongs to your AWS account and AWS Region, not to a knowledge base, and goes through these stages:

  • Create – 
    CreateRetrievalInstruction
    returns HTTP 202.
  • Review – Amazon Bedrock reviews the instruction’s fields asynchronously, and you poll for the result. If the review fails, 
    lastTransitionStatusReasons
    says why.
  • Activate – A passing review makes the instruction 
    ACTIVE
    , and 
    DRAFT
    points to its current content.
  • Version – 
    CreateRetrievalInstructionVersion
    saves an immutable numbered version.
  • Apply – A request names the instruction and, optionally, a version, which defaults to 
    DRAFT
    .
  • Report – The first 
    Planning
    trace event includes 
    appliedInstruction
    .

Scope and trade-offs

Instructions set voice, format, conventions, and policy wording. They don’t limit which documents the agent can retrieve, and they don’t choose the tenant’s own values, which come from naming the tenant in the request. Use metadata filters or separate knowledge bases to limit what each tenant can retrieve.

Solution overview

Each tenant gets its own instruction and metadata filter. The instruction sets the voice, format, and policy of the answer, and the filter limits which documents the agent retrieves. Your backend chooses both from the authenticated tenant, so one shared knowledge base can serve every tenant. In Figure 1, your backend maps the authenticated tenant to an instruction version and a metadata filter, and adds a short tenant line to the message. Then it calls 

AgenticRetrieveStream
on one shared managed knowledge base.

The same pattern works with a separate knowledge base for each tenant. A request can query a shared global knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base together, each with its own filter.

The example uses 32 short, fictitious AnyCompany Smart Home policy and product documents for the AnySmartProduct-5 home controller and AnySmartProduct-6 room sensors. They’re stored in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket, and each has 

region
, 
audience_team
, and 
sensitivity
metadata. Each of the six tenants, three regions and three teams, has its own instruction pinned to version 1. Two restricted engineering notes belong to no tenant, so no tenant’s filter should return them.

The code is in the GitHub repo, in Python and TypeScript, and runs in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) by default. To use another AWS Region, set 

AWS_REGION
. For the latest Region support, see Supported AWS Regions.

Prerequisites

You need the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create retrieval instructions, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and an S3 bucket.
  • One or more managed knowledge bases, with a metadata file for each document you want to filter on.
  • Python 3.10 or later and a current version of the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3). Older Boto3 versions don’t include the retrieval instruction operations.
  • A current version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) for control-plane commands. 
    AgenticRetrieveStream
    has no CLI command, so call it through an SDK.
  • Optional: an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, if you want to encrypt instructions with your own key.

Examples use Python with these two clients. Later snippets leave out the client setup and import lines.

Create a retrieval instruction for each tenant

The Sales Region Central instruction sets the language, date and money formats, and policy wording:

To create and pin each tenant’s instruction:

  • Select a tenant key, such as 
    sales-region-central
    , for the name and the 
    tenant
    tag.
  • Enter the instruction fields for that tenant.
  • Send 
    CreateRetrievalInstruction
    with the content and tags.
  • Poll 
    GetRetrievalInstruction
    until 
    lastTransitionStatus
    is neither 
    CREATING
    nor 
    UPDATING
    .
  • If the status isn’t 
    ACTIVE
    , read 
    lastTransitionStatusReasons
    , revise, and update.
  • Create a version and record it in your release configuration.

This code runs steps 3 and 6. The repo version adds the polling for steps 4 and 5.

An update replaces the whole instruction, including the description, so resend every field you want to keep. To encrypt an instruction with your own key, set 

customerEncryptionKeyArn
when you create it. You can’t add or change the key later. Your key policy also needs the statement in Encryption of retrieval instructions.

Keep tenant data apart with metadata filters

An instruction doesn’t limit which documents the agent retrieves. On a shared knowledge base, a Sales Region North customer’s question can return the Sales Region Central and South addenda, and even notes that no tenant should see. To keep each tenant to its own documents, add a metadata filter built from the authenticated tenant, or give the tenant its own knowledge base. A request can still query the tenant’s knowledge base alongside shared ones. Figure 2 compares the three approaches.

A metadata filter keeps one knowledge base to sync and maintain, but every document needs accurate metadata, and your backend must build the filter correctly on every request. A separate knowledge base per tenant isolates tenant data by design, but each tenant adds a knowledge base and data source to create, sync, and pay for. You can combine them: one request can query a shared knowledge base and the tenant’s own knowledge base, each with its own filter.

With a tenant filter or a separate knowledge base, the agent retrieves only documents the tenant is entitled to, so answers don’t quote other regions’ values. An answer policy that limits the assistant to one region helps, but without a filter an answer can still quote another region’s value.

Build the filter on your server from the authenticated tenant, because Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends:

This filter uses the 

equals
, 
andAll
, and 
orAll
operators on document metadata. It isn’t per-user access filtering through 
userContext
.

Answer policies are best effort. A line such as “Never share restricted engineering notes” can keep values out of the answer. If the notes are retrieved, though, an answer can still name the mechanism or record ID. To keep restricted content out of answers, exclude it with a metadata filter.

Answer as the tenant

For each request, your backend sends the tenant’s instruction ID and version, the tenant filter, and a tenant line. A tenant line is a short sentence, such as 

Customer sales region: Sales Region Central.
, placed before the question:

Here’s the same return question answered with three tenant instructions on one knowledge base, trimmed:

A tenant line tells the agent who is asking, which helps the answer quote that tenant’s values. It doesn’t set the tenant’s language, answer format, or date and money formats, so pair it with the tenant’s instruction. Without the instruction, a Sales Region Central answer can come back in English, without the 

Source:
line, or in the wrong date format.

Without an instruction, a customer answer can also quote internal discount tiers from a document the tenant can retrieve. An answer policy that forbids them, like the Sales Region Central one, can keep them out, but to make sure, filter out the document that contains them. Team formats such as the ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer, so validate the format in any code that depends on it.

Instructions change how an answer is written. The facts still come from the documents the agent retrieves, so compute exact values such as a return deadline in your application.

Cover users who belong to a region and a team

A request can reference only one retrieval instruction. When a user belongs to both a region and a team, that instruction has to cover both. For example, a support agent in Sales Region South needs the support team’s voice and the region’s date and money formats. Table 2 compares two ways to set that up for N regions and M teams.

ApproachInstructions to maintainApplies the region’s formats
One combined instruction for each region and team pairN x M, plus the N region and M team instructions you already haveYes
The team’s instruction, with the region named in the tenant lineN + MNo, the team’s formats apply

Table 2: Two ways to cover a region and a team with one instruction

Start with the team’s instruction and a region tenant line, which keeps the count at N + M. Add a combined instruction only for pairs whose formats differ from the team’s default. Neither approach limits what the agent retrieves, so keep the tenant filter on every request. A filter also can’t remove a value from a shared document the tenant is entitled to, such as a global policy that lists every region’s dates. As of this writing, the default quota is 50 retrieval instructions per account per AWS Region, and you can request an increase. Combined instructions add up quickly, with 15 for 3 regions and 3 teams and 65 for 10 regions and 5 teams.

Scope tenant roles with instruction tags

If your application calls agentic retrieval with the same role for every tenant, IAM can’t tell tenants apart, and your code alone chooses each request’s instruction and filter. When each tenant’s requests run under that tenant’s own credentials, tag conditions add a second check on which instruction a request can apply and who can change it. Those credentials can come from a role per tenant or a role assumed with a tenant session tag.

AgenticRetrieveStream
has no IAM resource. To apply an instruction, the caller needs 
bedrock:GetRetrievalInstruction
on the instruction’s Amazon Resource Name (ARN), so that’s where the tag condition goes. These attribute-based access control (ABAC) statements from the example’s AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) app scope one tenant:

With these statements, a tenant’s applier role can apply only instructions tagged with its tenant, and its tenant admin role can manage only those instructions. The platform admin can manage any tenant’s instructions. Require both tag conditions on 

TagResource
. With only the request-tag condition, a tenant admin can retag another tenant’s instruction into its own scope. To add a tenant, add its key to the 
tenantRoles
context value and deploy the AWS CDK app again with the same 
trustedPrincipalArn
. Apply permission doesn’t limit retrieval, so scope 
bedrock:Retrieve
to each role’s knowledge bases. 
ListRetrievalInstructions
can’t be scoped by tag, so keep instruction names free of sensitive information.

Trace each answer to a tenant and version

As Use retrieval instructions with agentic retrieval describes, the first 

Planning
trace event includes 
appliedInstruction
, with the ID and version of the instruction that was applied. Log it with the tenant ID:

For every event type, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference. To capture the applied instruction, check for the first 

Planning
event in the loop that reads the answer:

For an audit record outside your application, use AWS CloudTrail. CloudTrail logs Agents for Amazon Bedrock Runtime operations, including 

AgenticRetrieveStream
, as data events. A trail records data events only after you enable them. For details, see Monitor Amazon Bedrock API calls using CloudTrail.

Release instruction changes one tenant at a time

Amazon Bedrock doesn’t route traffic between versions. Keep a release configuration for each tenant, pin its version on every request, and canary, promote, or roll back by changing that pin. The trace confirms which version served each request, not whether the new version answers better, so gate each promotion on your own checks. This release configuration is from the repo’s router:

To change one tenant, update its instruction, wait for the review, create a version, and move only that tenant’s pin. For example, moving the support tenant to version 2 leaves the other five tenants on version 1:

A pin fixes the instruction, not the exact wording of each answer. During an update review, 

DRAFT
keeps serving the previous content. A version create or a second update during the review fails with HTTP 409, so poll until the review finishes, as the retrieval instruction rollout steps describe.

More ways to use retrieval instructions

Retrieval instructions aren’t only for multi-tenant setups. The same fields work for a single application, such as an assistant that has to return JSON for downstream code or keep one voice across every answer. The repo has code for the first three.

Return structured JSON

An 

answerFormat
can replace your own generation step:

With this 

answerFormat
, agentic retrieval can return the JSON directly, so you don’t need a separate generation step. Validate the JSON in your code before you use it.

Serve several audiences

Give each audience its own 

persona
and 
answerFormat
, such as a customer answer and a ticket note, so the same knowledge bases can serve them all without mixing their formats.

Apply one instruction across knowledge bases

Several retrievers can share one instruction version:

Keep a consistent brand voice

Set identity, tone, and language once in 

persona
, such as “Use a friendly, concise tone. Reply in the language of the question.”

Add disclaimers or citation formats

Put required lines in 

answerPolicy
and citation forms in 
answerFormat
, and give a realistic citation example, such as 
Source: central-returns-addendum.md
, instead of a placeholder.

Hand off questions outside scope

Use 

answerPolicy
to name the fallback, such as “If the documents do not answer the question, say so and give the support contact.”

Teach domain vocabulary

Use 

retrievalGuidance
for acronyms and preferred sources, such as “Treat model numbers as exact-match terms.” Check the 
Planning
trace events to see how the agent searched. Use filters, not guidance, to limit what it retrieves.

Best practices for writing retrieval instructions

Follow these practices when you write and roll out retrieval instructions:

  • Add a tenant line to the message. It helps the answer quote the tenant’s own values.
  • Bind filters to the authenticated tenant on the server. Amazon Bedrock applies whatever filter the request sends.
  • Pin versions in production. Test on 
    DRAFT
    , then promote by changing the pin.
  • Wait for each review to finish. After a create or update, poll until the review succeeds before you create a version. A version create during a review fails with HTTP 409.
  • Treat answer policies as best effort. To keep a documented fact out of answers, filter out the document that contains it.
  • Validate formats your code depends on. Formats such as a ticket note aren’t guaranteed on every answer.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the retrieval instructions with the following commands. Then follow the cleanup steps in the repo README for the knowledge base, data source, S3 bucket, and roles.

Conclusion

Retrieval instructions give each tenant its own voice, answer format, date and money formats, and answer policy on shared managed knowledge bases. Pair them with metadata filters to keep tenant data apart and pinned versions to roll out changes one tenant at a time. The trace shows which version answered, and CloudTrail can record the 

AgenticRetrieveStream
calls. Tag conditions add a check when tenants have their own credentials.

To get started, see the AgenticRetrieveStream API reference and the GitHub repo. To learn more, read Agentic retrieval for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base.

entries.summary: Many generative AI applications resend the same long context on every request. Prompt caching lets open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock reuse it to reduce input cost and latency. This post shows implicit and explicit caching through the Chat Completions API and applies caching to an OpenCode coding agent session.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Use prompt caching with open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock

Many generative AI applications send the same long context with every request, and prompt caching avoids processing it again each time. That context can be a system prompt, reference documents, tool definitions, or the conversation so far. Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock can reuse it across requests, which helps reduce input costs and response latency.

Prompt caching reuses the computed state of a matching prompt prefix, so repeated context is read from cache instead of being processed again. Amazon Bedrock manages the cache for you. Depending on the model, you can use implicit caching, which works automatically, explicit caching, where you mark the reusable prefix, or both. The more context you reuse, and the more often you reuse it, the more you can save.

As with other models on Amazon Bedrock, your prompts and outputs aren’t shared with the model provider or used to train models. For more information, see Data protection in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

Open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock now support explicit prompt caching. In this post, we use both modes with an open-weight model through the Chat Completions API and show how to read cache usage from each response. We then apply implicit caching to an OpenCode coding agent session on the same API and close with best practices.

Prompt caching for open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock

When a request starts with the same content as an earlier one, Amazon Bedrock reads that prefix from cache and processes only the rest. Cache reads are billed at a lower rate than standard input, so the savings can grow each time a prefix is reused. Depending on the model, cache writes can be billed at a higher rate than standard input. See Amazon Bedrock pricing for the rates of each model.

Supported modes depend on the model and the API. For each model’s caching modes, minimum prefix length, and how long entries stay cached, see Models at a glance. The two modes compare as follows:

FeatureImplicit cachingExplicit caching
Request changesNoneOn the Chat Completions API, 
prompt_cache_options
with mode set to explicit, plus one or more 
prompt_cache_breakpoint
markers
What is cachedEligible prefixes, selected automatically on a best-effort basisContent up to and including each breakpoint
Good fitPrompts that already start with a stable prefix, such as conversations and agent loopsA fixed shared prefix with a changing question, or layered prefixes that you want to control

Implicit caching: Amazon Bedrock reuses eligible prefixes automatically, on a best-effort basis. In a conversation, each request resends the full context, so the previous request becomes the cached prefix of the next one (Figure 1). As the prompt caching guide recommends, put static content first and dynamic content last. Keeping the start of the prompt stable lets every later request reuse it. If an early part changes, as in turn 4 of Figure 1, the cache is rebuilt from that point.

Explicit caching: You mark the end of each reusable prefix with a cache breakpoint. You can add several breakpoints, up to the maximum that the model supports, to cache layers that change at different rates, as Figure 2 shows. Content up to each breakpoint is written to cache once and then read on later requests, and content after the last breakpoint is processed on each request. Check the model card for the minimum token count before a breakpoint, the maximum number of breakpoints, and the time to live (TTL), which resets with each cache hit.

With implicit caching, Amazon Bedrock can also write content to cache that later requests never reuse, such as a question that’s different each time. When the content after a shared prefix changes on every request, use explicit caching to limit cache writes to the shared prefix. Content after the last breakpoint is billed at the standard input rate. On models that charge more for cache writes, you don’t pay the higher write rate for content that’s never read back.

Solution overview

The following diagram shows how both examples in this post reach Amazon Bedrock through the same Chat Completions API endpoint.

  • The Python application and the OpenCode coding agent send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your Region, authenticated with a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key.
  • Amazon Bedrock checks the prompt cache for a matching prefix. It reads a matching prefix from cache, and writes new cacheable content to cache.
  • Amazon Bedrock sends the request to the selected open-weight model and returns the response, including the cache usage fields that the following sections show you how to read.

Prerequisites

To run the samples, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with access to your selected model on Amazon Bedrock. Model availability and prompt caching support vary by AWS Region, so check the model card for the Regions that your model supports.
  • AWS credentials for an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity that has permission to invoke your selected model on Amazon Bedrock.
  • Python 3.12 with the 
    openai
    (3.26.0 or later) and 
    aws-bedrock-token-generator
    (1.1.0 or later) packages.
  • For the coding agent example, npm to install OpenCode 1.18.35.

Before you use a model, review its license and service terms, linked from its model card. Your use of the model is also subject to the AWS Responsible AI Policy.

Cache a product manual through the Chat Completions API

The example is a support assistant for a fictional water filter, the AnyCompany AquaPure 500. The system prompt holds a one-line instruction and the owner’s manual, which is the reusable prefix. Each request asks a different customer question.

Set up the client

The samples use the OpenAI Python SDK with the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint. For authentication, the 

provide_token()
function from the 
aws-bedrock-token-generator
package turns your AWS credentials into a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key, valid for up to 12 hours. You don’t need to create or store a long-term key.

1. Create a virtual environment and install the packages:

2. Create the manual. Ours is about 4,000 tokens of Markdown. The following excerpt shows its format:

Save it as 

manual.md
and add sections until it’s longer than the minimum prefix length on your model card. Placeholder text works, because the cache only needs an identical prefix. Keep the three sections shown, which answer the sample questions.

3. Save the following setup code as 

common.py
in the same directory. The samples that you create next import from it.

If your model returns reasoning tokens, they count toward 

max_tokens
. The samples set 
max_tokens=1024
so that short answers have room to finish.

Implicit caching

Implicit caching takes no cache controls. Put the manual in the system message and the question in the user message. Sending both as parts of one user message got no implicit cache hits. Save the following as 

implicit.py
and run it with 
python implicit.py
:

Verify implicit caching

Each response reports cache activity in 

usage.prompt_tokens_details
. Figure 4 shows how to read these fields and the pattern to expect across the three calls of each sample.

In implicit mode, call 1 writes the prompt to cache. Calls 2 and 3 read the system message, with the instruction and the manual, back from cache. They also write a few tokens each, because implicit mode extends the cached prefix to cover each new question. A few tokens after the last message stay uncached on every call. This is the pattern for the first run. If you run the sample again within the TTL, every call reads from cache, and none writes.

Explicit caching

Choose explicit caching to control exactly what is cached. As Figure 4 shows, calls 2 and 3 of the implicit run each write a few tokens to cache, whereas the same calls with explicit caching write nothing. With several breakpoints, you can cache layered prefixes, such as shared instructions and tools followed by a per-customer document (Figure 2).

For explicit caching, add the following to the request:

  • prompt_cache_options
    with mode set to explicit selects explicit mode. It’s an Amazon Bedrock request field, and the OpenAI SDK sends it through 
    extra_body
    .
  • prompt_cache_breakpoint
    on a text content part marks the end of the reusable prefix. Content up to and including that part is cached, and content after it’s processed again on every request.

Save the explicit version of the same loop as 

explicit.py
:

Set both parts together. Explicit mode without a breakpoint caches nothing, and a breakpoint without explicit mode behaves like implicit caching. For the optional 

ttl
field of 
prompt_cache_options
, check the model card for supported values.

Verify explicit caching

If you run 

explicit.py
right after 
implicit.py
, its first call is already a cache hit. For a cold first call, add a unique first line to the system prompt, for example 
SYSTEM_PROMPT = f"Run ID: {uuid.uuid4()}\n" + SYSTEM_PROMPT
(with 
import uuid
at the top of 
explicit.py
).

As the explicit bars in Figure 4 show, only the first call writes. Each repeat reads the whole prefix up to the breakpoint and writes nothing, and the question after the breakpoint makes up the uncached remainder.

Use prompt caching with the OpenCode coding agent

Coding agents resend a large, stable prefix on every step: the system prompt, tool definitions, and the conversation so far. That makes them a natural fit for implicit caching. OpenCode is an open source coding agent. It can call any Chat Completions endpoint through a custom OpenAI-compatible provider, so it can use the same Amazon Bedrock endpoint as the Python samples. Figure 5 shows the requests that OpenCode sends during one turn and which parts Amazon Bedrock reads from cache.

In one turn, OpenCode sends request 1 with its system prompt, tool definitions, and your prompt, and Amazon Bedrock writes it to cache. The model responds with a tool call, which OpenCode runs on your machine. OpenCode then sends request 2, which contains request 1 plus the tool call and its result. Amazon Bedrock reads request 1 from cache, writes only the new tail, and returns the response.

Configure OpenCode

Install OpenCode and check the version:

Next, add the following 

opencode.json
to the root of your repository, or save it as 
~/.config/opencode/opencode.json
to apply it to every project. It defines a provider named 
bedrock
that uses the OpenAI-compatible package to call the Amazon Bedrock Chat Completions endpoint:

OpenCode uses 

small_model
for session titles, so pointing it at the same model keeps every request on a model that you’ve enabled. The provider reads its key from 
BEDROCK_API_KEY
. Set it to a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from 
provide_token()
, in the virtual environment from the first example. If the key expires, run the command again to get a new one:

Confirm that OpenCode lists the model:

Verify implicit caching in a coding session

We ran a three-turn session against a small repository that holds one short Python file. Turn 1 asks for a bug review, turn 2 for a fix, and turn 3 for a short follow-up:

Replace

with the 
sessionID
value from the JSON output of turn 1. The 
opencode export
command lists each request’s token usage: 
cache.read
holds the 
cached_tokens
value from Amazon Bedrock, and 
input
holds the rest. OpenCode 1.18.35 doesn’t record 
cache_write_tokens
for an OpenAI-compatible provider, so 
cache.write
stays at 0.

Figure 6 shows how much of each request in the session is read from cache.

The first request processes the whole prompt, most of it the OpenCode system prompt and tool definitions, and Amazon Bedrock writes it to cache. Each later request reads everything up to the end of the previous request from cache, so only the new tail of the conversation is processed. This works with no caching configuration.

Best practices

These practices apply to any model that supports prompt caching:

  • Put static content first, in both modes. Place the system prompt, tool definitions, and reference documents before content that changes, and keep them identical between requests. In explicit mode, place each breakpoint after the static content that it covers. Timestamps and request IDs belong at the end of the prompt.
  • Make the prefix long enough. Prefixes that meet the minimum token count on the model card are eligible for caching.
  • Confirm hits with the usage fields. Check the cache reads and writes in each response, in either mode. Across a workload, track the 
    CacheReadInputTokenCount
    and 
    CacheWriteInputTokenCount
    runtime metrics.
  • Keep the cache warm. Steady traffic keeps a prefix cached, because the TTL resets with each hit. After an idle gap longer than the TTL, the next request writes the prefix again.
  • Cache what you reuse. Savings come from cache reads, so cache content that later requests read again, especially where cache writes cost more than standard input. With cross-Region inference, expect some extra cache writes at times of high demand.

Clean up

The examples make inference calls only and create no resources in your AWS account. Cache entries expire after they go unread for the TTL. The short-term API key from 

provide_token()
also expires on its own, and the samples never write it to disk. To clear it from your shell sooner, run 
unset BEDROCK_API_KEY
.

To remove the local files:

1. Delete the sample directory and its Python virtual environment.

2. Delete 

opencode.json
from your repository, or 
~/.config/opencode/opencode.json
if you saved it globally.

3. If you no longer need OpenCode, delete 

~/.local/opt/opencode
.

Conclusion

Prompt caching lets open-weight models on Amazon Bedrock reuse repeated context with little or no change to your code. In this post, implicit caching covered the support assistant and the OpenCode session with no cache settings at all. Explicit caching gave precise control with one request option and a breakpoint for each reusable layer. In every case, the usage fields on each response show what came from cache, so you can measure the benefit on your own traffic.

To get started, choose an open-weight model on Amazon Bedrock that supports prompt caching. Run the samples from this post with your own reference content, and compare the cache reads with your uncached input. The prompt caching guide covers the limits and options for each model, and the Amazon Bedrock runtime metrics let you track cache reads and writes across your applications. For questions, reach out through AWS Support or the AWS re:Post community.
